+ Classic sci-fi: The Azra Gambit — Score: 71.8
Prompt:
Classic sci-fi (Author style: Asimov) The Azra Gambit Colonial mars is being mined by corporations who take leases on indentured labourers. The thing they are mining is Azra, a recently discovered exotic metal which accelerates radioactive decay to such a rate that it is greatly sought after for interstellar drives and weapons alike. This has created both a gold rush and an arms race as various interests vie for control and endeavour to unlock Azra's secrets. The story follows Arthur Neegan, a first generation settler and mining engineer. Upon discovering that his unassuming plot sits atop an immense Azra vein, he is subjected to a flurry of interest and scrutiny. Write the next chapter in this story, in which an armed retinue descends on Arthur's home and politely but forcefully invites him to a meeting with some unknown party off-world. The insignia look like that of the Antares diplomatic corp -- diplomatic in name only. Arthur finds himself in the centre of a political tug of war. The chapter involves a meeting with this unknown party, who makes Arthur an offer. The scene should be primarily dialogue, interspersed with vivid description & scene setting. It should sow hints of the larger intrigue, stakes & dangers. Include Asimov's trademark big-and-small-picture world building and retrofuturistic classic scifi vibe. The chapter begins with Arthur aboard the transfer vessel, wondering just what he's gotten involved in. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
## The Convenient Invitation Arthur kept adjusting his collar as the transfer vessel *Cynthia B.* rolled with the gentle, unreasonable motion of a ship changing course. The black tunic had been pressed aboard, stiff enough to stand unaided. He was thirty-one, a mining engineer, and a first-generation Martian—which meant, as his father liked to say, that Earth was a country he had never governed. He had a small house beneath two tons of regolith and sixty-one people dependent on his claim. Twenty hours ago, armed men had arrived to explain that all three were now negotiable. They had been unusually polite about it. Six of them had descended from the morning shuttle wearing grey uniforms and compact needle carbines. Their insignia was a gold sunburst enclosing a blue-white star: Antares Diplomatic Corps, according to the woman who spoke. “Mr. Neegan, the Corps requests your presence at an off-world meeting concerning your property.” “I’d like to see the request.” “You are seeing it.” “The rest?” “Off-world.” At that range, Arthur had observed, the distinction between an invitation and an instruction was largely terminological. The woman had introduced herself as Prefect Voss. She had not threatened his family, searched his house, or helped herself to his survey instruments. Instead, two of her men had quietly taken possession of the power controls while another stood beside Arthur’s core samples. “You have a comfortable ship,” Arthur had said. “We are told you will find it comfortable.” The sample case had come with him. So had the collar. He suspected these were related only in the minds of people who wished to make him comfortable. The *Cynthia B.* had no observation port. That was technically a docking port, Voss explained, but the distinction did not comfort him. The cabin possessed the air of an expensive terrestrial hotel: indirect lighting, synthetic wood panelling, a narrow bed, and a pitcher of water with the assurance that it contained no minerals worth stealing. The food was perfectly prepared and flavoured with nothing Arthur could identify. They had spent the first six hours beyond Mars orbit, then rendezvoused with a larger vessel. Now, through the meeting room’s single broad window, he could see only the curve of Mars. It filled half the sky, ochre and white and seemingly close enough to touch. In reality, someone had told him during the voyage, it was some two hundred kilometres away. Yet the dome lights along his property, barely distinguishable, seemed to shine in the same room with him. Earth was another matter. Earth was a memory, a market, and, increasingly, a creditor. He was still puzzling over the implications of the armed hospitality when the door opened. “You must be Arthur Neegan,” said the man beyond it. “The engineer, not the public figure. How fortunate that they are so nearly indistinguishable.” Arthur rose. “You have the advantage.” “Director Dardin, special envoy. At the moment, that is all I can safely be.” Dardin was perhaps sixty, broad and silver-haired, dressed in a suit that had survived the journey without a wrinkle. His eyes moved over Arthur’s borrowed tunic with polite disappointment. “I trust the accommodations were satisfactory?” “Your ship has excellent taste in collars and poor taste in not providing windows.” “A diplomatic asset. One must learn to conduct important business without the distraction of scenery.” Dardin sat. “Would you care to drink something that is not a mineral solution?” “Coffee.” “Of course.” The coffee arrived, hot and black and unmistakably real. Arthur had last tasted it three years before, at his father’s funeral. Dardin watched him take it. “You are wondering what you have become involved in.” “No. I decided that before boarding.” “Then you are ahead of most engineers.” You have a discovery that people want to kill for, Dardin said. That is not quite the same thing. People want to kill for many things, but usually they begin with the things they cannot otherwise obtain. Arthur set down the cup. “What is that, in this case?” Dardin placed a thin data slate on the table. “Eighty million credits.” Arthur waited. He had acquired the habit, during negotiations over machinery and labour, of letting silence do the first round of work. “Paid not in ordinary credits,” Dardin continued, “but in oxygen bonds and registered mining shares. There are enough bonds to provide breathable air to every registered resident on your lease for twenty years. The shares carry an eighty-percent return guaranteed by Antares Development Combine.” Arthur read the figures. They were even more impressive in the absence of context. “And the workers?” “Their contracts are reviewed. All illegitimate debt clauses are cancelled. Each family receives a residential claim in its own name.” “*Illegitimate?*” “There is a technical distinction.” “In other words, you’ll pay their debts.” “They become your beneficiaries.” “And in return?” “Your mineral claim, assay records, and survey data. A seven-year operating lease on the vein. The right to purchase your workers’ production at a fixed price.” The price was generous. Dangerously so. “There’s more,” said Dardin. “There usually is.” “We intend to finance a Martian government with universal suffrage, property protections, and a foreign policy independent of Earth. You would be one of its founding electors.” Arthur looked up. “You’re buying my vote.” “We are investing in your judgment. We would also finance your campaign for the Assembly.” “You didn’t buy my vote.” “Yet.” Dardin took a drink of his coffee. Outside, Mars turned slowly, carrying clouds and cities and a billion human arguments around the same battered planet. “You own an enormous deposit,” Arthur said. “We do not need the deposit.” “Then why are you here?” “Because you did more than discover it.” Dardin turned the slate around. A legal document appeared, dense with clauses. “In eight days, the Earth Ministry of Resources intends to introduce an emergency common-ground bill. The central parcel of each deposit would become the legal key to every surrounding claim. Whoever owns it could license, veto, or absorb them all.” Arthur read paragraph nineteen. “This is the mineral lease I signed six years ago.” “Appendix eleven, subsection four. You filed the survey automatically when you registered the well. I imagine you never read that far.” “No.” “Most people don’t. It is a useful little lesson in the value of literacy.” “So Earth wants to take my claim.” “Earth wants to ensure that no Martian owns anything important without Earth’s permission.” Dardin’s voice remained mild. “The Ministry calls it stabilization. The Combine calls it civilization. The Freeholders call it theft. We simply point out that a colony capable of governing itself requires more than a surface.” Arthur understood the larger picture. Earth possessed the industry, the fleets, and the accumulated political machinery of several centuries. Mars possessed the rocks, the labour, and a stubborn conviction that distance constituted a government. The trouble was that both sides preferred the other to remain unfinished. “And your interest?” “Order, Mr. Neegan. Cheap order is our business.” Arthur picked up the contract. A silver seal marked the door: a gold sunburst with thirteen rays. He noticed because his mother had been a cartographer. She had taught him that a map’s most dangerous feature was usually the mistake no one else had seen. Dardin followed his gaze. “A variation of the traditional insignia,” he said. “Do you know the traditional one has twelve rays?” “Old habits die hard.” Arthur returned to the contract. “If I refuse?” “Then the Combine will purchase the debt of your tenants. It will close the atmospheric plant unless you surrender voting rights. It will place guards at the railway and call them security. Within a year, your claim will belong to the Ministry, your workers will belong to the Combine, and you will be free to explain to the latter what freedom cost.” “Not much of a choice.” “It is the only choice. We merely arrange for both alternatives to have our fingerprints on them.” Arthur looked again at the thirteen-rayed star. “One more condition,” he said. “I want assurances that my people can leave Mars without your consent.” Dardin smiled. “You have just discovered the principal difference between a government and a corporation. One permits its citizens to emigrate. The other charges them for the opportunity.” At that moment, a light appeared over the door. “Sir,” said Voss, “the transfer vessel has completed its external checks. It must undock in twenty-eight minutes.” Dardin did not turn around. “Thank you, Prefect.” Arthur looked through the window. The *Cynthia B.* was already drawing away, shrinking into the darkness between Mars and its moons. Its passenger compartment was lit, warm, and empty. “So that,” he said, “was not really the return ticket.” “It was never intended to be.” “Where is it going?” “For now, the outer shipyards. Its next scheduled run to Mars is in four months.” Arthur took a breath. Somewhere below him, his house waited beneath its patient roof. His workers were waking for the morning shift, trusting that the ore they touched still belonged to the man who had found it. Dardin pushed the contract across the table. “Shall we discuss the price of your cooperation?” Arthur looked at the pen, the elegant clothing, the armed ship waiting beyond reach. “I think,” he said, “the price is still being decided.” For the first time, Dardin’s expression disturbed him more than the guns had. It was the expression of a man who had been given to understand exactly what that meant.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical competence and successfully captures many elements of Asimov's style, particularly the focus on political machinations, clear prose, and dialogue-driven exposition. The author effectively establishes the retrofuturistic setting with details like needle carbines, oxygen bonds, and atmospheric plants, while maintaining the clinical, analytical tone characteristic of classic science fiction. The dialogue serves multiple functions well - advancing plot, revealing character motivations, and exposing the larger political situation. Dardin emerges as a compelling antagonist who presents reasonable arguments while maintaining an underlying menace. Arthur's responses feel authentic for an engineer caught in circumstances beyond his control, though his characterization could be deeper. The world-building successfully hints at larger conflicts between Earth and Mars without overwhelming the immediate scene. The detail about the thirteen-rayed star versus the traditional twelve is a nice touch that suggests deeper deceptions. The political situation - Earth's attempt to control Martian resources through legal manipulation - feels plausible and mirrors historical colonial dynamics. However, the piece has notable weaknesses. The pacing drags in places, particularly in the opening sections aboard the ship. Some descriptions feel unnecessarily elaborate for Asimov's typically spare style. The ending, while dramatically appropriate, lacks the punch of revelation or choice that would make it truly compelling. The characterization of Arthur remains somewhat surface-level. While his responses are believable, we don't get a strong sense of his internal conflict or emotional state beyond wariness. The stakes are clearly established but don't feel viscerally urgent. The prose is generally competent but occasionally becomes overwrought, particularly in descriptive passages that don't serve the narrative momentum. Some dialogue exchanges feel slightly artificial in their precision, though this may be intentional given the diplomatic setting. + Contemporary romance: Darkroom Revelations — Score: 88.8
Prompt:
Darkroom Revelations Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of Dani, a 25-year-old assertive art student known for her bold style and take-charge attitude in relationships. For the past semester, she's been quietly fascinated by Elliot (he/him), a 19-year-old boy in her experimental photography class. Dani has been intrigued by his unconventional masculinity: killer thrift-shop-nu-goth style, soft demeanour and quiet intellect. When they're paired for a final project requiring late nights in the darkroom, Elliot tentatively shares that he's been questioning his gender identity and expression. Set during one of these intimate darkroom sessions where the red light creates a confessional atmosphere. Explore Dani's complex attraction—her usual assertiveness complicated by her desire to protect Elliot's vulnerability, her excitement at witnessing his self-discovery, and her confusion about what this means for her own identity as someone typically attracted to more defined gender presentations. The narrative should capture the tender awkwardness of their conversations, Dani's internal struggle between taking charge and wanting to give Elliot agency, and the unexpected chemistry that develops as both find themselves in uncharted territory. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Darkroom Revelations By the third week, the darkroom had become a country with no daylight. It smelled of stop bath, wet cardboard, and the metallic ghost of fixer. Under the safelight, our hands looked anatomical, blood reduced to ink. Elliot and I stood on either side of the developing tray, waiting for a photograph to admit it existed. He was nineteen. I was twenty-five. I usually filled rooms myself: white shirt buttoned to the throat, red nails, posture that said *Give me a reason*. In relationships, I liked women whose certainty met mine halfway. Elliot met nothing halfway. He met it carefully. His long black thrift-shop coat, layered mesh, and mismatched silver rings gave him the sharp silhouette of a villain in a film about saints. Beneath all that, he spoke softly. When he concentrated, he folded one hand around the other wrist, holding himself with improbable gentleness. People stared at his clothes. He seemed mostly interested in making sure they were comfortable. The contrast had snagged in me long before we were paired. Our project required a portrait that resisted explanation. He kept tilting his head at the empty background, rearranging the lights, then asking whether a composition was too on the nose. I admired his precision, and the hollow of his throat when he leaned over the loupe. I resented how little I trusted my own motives. That night, after the enlarger clicked twice, he set down the print with unusual care. “Can I tell you something that isn’t about the project?” I should have said *of course*, the brisk reassurance I gave everyone. Instead, because he looked at the red light instead of me, I said, “Tell me.” “Everyone calls me he,” he said. “I do too. Mostly, it fits. But lately it feels like only part of the answer. I thought if I found the right clothes, the right way of moving, I’d know whether I was a guy. I don’t.” He stopped, fingers worrying the hem of his sleeve. “Sometimes I wonder if it’s my gender. Sometimes I think it’s just how I express it. Sometimes I don’t know what I’m looking at.” The urge to solve him rose in me, clean and immediate. I wanted to ask what names he’d considered, what he felt when people used the wrong ones, whether a word existed that fixed the wrongness. I wanted to give him an elegant theory. Instead, I heard the effort beneath his voice and kept my questions to myself. “You don’t have to know tonight,” I said. “Or tomorrow. Not for me.” He finally looked up. “That’s different.” “Is it bad?” “No. I don’t think anyone’s asked me that before.” His shoulders loosened. I understood, then, that protecting his vulnerability did not mean pretending he couldn’t bear its weight. It meant not making my curiosity heavier than his need. I reached for the enlarger, then stopped. I could take over: choose the filter, adjust the shadows, make him indisputably beautiful. I wanted to find out what it meant to take charge of the space without taking him over. “What do you want the portrait to hold?” I asked. “Me,” he said. “Before I have words for the rest of me.” “Hands first, then,” I said. “Can you show me what that looks like?” He nodded. I made him say *yes* before I moved his sleeve from his wrist. The request changed the air. I had expected the image to challenge my preferences. I hadn’t expected the permission to undo me. He stood beneath the enlarger, a velvet hanger against one palm. Light found the ridges of his knuckles, the silver at his throat, the faint shadow where shaving had grazed his jaw. I raised the camera. Something fierce and protective moved through me. I wanted everyone to see his courage. But wanting to display someone’s bravery could be another way of owning it. So I framed him instead. I softened the lamp and asked, “Are you all right?” “I am,” he said. “It feels strange, but yes.” I lowered the shutter. The photograph, surfacing in the tray, caught him neither masked nor revealed. He was simply arriving. “I thought it would look more certain,” he said. “It looks more honest,” I said. He studied that. “Those aren’t always the same thing.” No, I thought. But they were here. When I passed him the second sheet, our fingers touched. I would once have let my hand linger, turned accident into proposition. This time I stayed still. He drew back, then laid his fingertips over mine. The touch was feather-light, almost exploratory. I let him keep it there until he decided the question was finished. My usual attractions arranged themselves in my memory: clear silhouettes, low voices, women who took up space without apology. Elliot didn’t replace them. He made me doubt how neatly I had sorted myself. Desire could be stranger than the stories I told about it, and attraction did not have to become a verdict before it could be true. I had mistaken definiteness for depth. He leaned close to inspect the drying print. “You’re different in here.” “So are you,” I replied. “Not enough to know yet.” “Do you want to know?” He considered. “Not tonight. I want to see what happens if I don’t decide.” I nodded. It cost more restraint than any critique had asked. “Okay,” I said. He smiled. “You’re good at this.” “Don’t get used to it.” He laughed, quiet and startled by the sound. My phone buzzed in my pocket, insisting on a bright world beyond the door. I ignored it. Outside, people waited for neat explanations, for bodies to fall into line with their categories. In here, the red light made every certainty look temporary. I let it. He lifted the last print by its edges. “This one looks like me,” he said. “Yes,” I said, and meant it without knowing what *yes* contained. The answer could wait. The portrait, at least, was ours. We hung it to drip in the dark, side by side, beneath the same red light. Nothing had to be named to be real.

The darkroom setting is expertly utilized both literally and metaphorically - the red light creates an intimate, confessional atmosphere while serving as a symbol for the liminal space both characters occupy. The photography metaphors are woven throughout naturally, enhancing rather than overwhelming the narrative. Character development is particularly strong. Dani's internal conflict between her usual take-charge approach and her recognition that Elliot needs agency is believable and well-rendered. Her self-reflection about her own identity and attractions feels authentic rather than forced. Elliot emerges as a fully realized character despite being seen through Dani's eyes - his vulnerability, style, and tentative self-exploration are convincingly portrayed. The prose style is elegant and controlled, with memorable phrases like "a country with no daylight" and "blood reduced to ink." The writing avoids purple prose while maintaining literary sophistication. Dialogue feels natural and serves character development effectively, particularly in the central conversation about gender identity. The emotional complexity is handled with nuance - Dani's attraction, protectiveness, confusion, and growth are layered convincingly. The piece avoids easy answers or rushed resolutions, instead embracing uncertainty as both characters navigate uncharted territory. The pacing is well-controlled, building intimacy gradually through shared work in the darkroom. The ending strikes an appropriate note - hopeful but not artificially positive, acknowledging that both characters are in process rather than providing neat closure. Minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the metaphorical language borders on being slightly overwrought, though it generally stays within bounds. The piece could have explored Dani's own identity questions slightly more deeply, though this may be a constraint of the word count. + Contemporary romance / drama: Stolen Moments in Roma — Score: 75.7
Prompt:
Contemporary Romance / Drama: Stolen Moments in Roma. Write a series of interconnected short scenes and dialogues that span a single day in modern-day Rome, in narrative form. This will form the beginning of a larger story. Alessandra, a fiery, independent Roman woman who works as a motorcycle courier, nearly collides with Ben, a somewhat clumsy, overly polite British academic on sabbatical, who is engrossed in a guidebook near the Trevi Fountain. The initial encounter is a clash of cultures and personalities – Alessandra is all sharp wit and rapid-fire Italian, while Ben is flustered apologies and awkward attempts at speaking the language. However, as they sort out the near-miss, a spark of unexpected humor and connection emerges. Alessandra, it quickly becomes clear, is a whirlwind of energy and mischief. She's a self-admitted troublemaker with a secret penchant for kleptomania, a detail she doesn't explicitly reveal, but which manifests in subtle, daring acts throughout the day. She impulsively decides to take Ben on a wild, unsanctioned tour of Rome, dragging him in some specific instances far outside his comfort zone. Ben, despite his initial apprehension and inherent politeness, finds himself utterly captivated by Alessandra's unapologetic spirit and zest for life. He is drawn into her orbit, a willing participant in increasingly outlandish situations, a quiet rebellion brewing beneath his scholarly exterior. The narrative should primarily consist of short, vivid scenes and dialogue exchanges, revealing their contrasting personalities and backgrounds, and the growing, ambiguous tension between them. Ben is captivated by Alessandra's energy and the thrill of breaking free from his routine. There's a clear sense that Alessandra is toying with Ben, pushing his boundaries and enjoying his reactions, but her own feelings remain somewhat enigmatic. The day should be a rollercoaster of exhilarating, slightly dangerous, and humorous moments, leaving Ben completely disoriented but utterly smitten. Explore the underlying tension & chemistry between them, culminating in some payoff as they part ways (or not -- your choice). Include this detail: Write in narrative prose, using immersive storytelling. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Stolen Moments in Roma Eight-seventeen in the morning, and the Trevi Fountain was already crowded with tourists and the sound of water pretending not to be in a hurry. Ben Mercer, a Cambridge historian on sabbatical, stood on the steps reading a secondhand guidebook. He had a book about medieval pilgrims to revise and a hotel breakfast to regret. He turned a page. A horn blared. A red motorcycle swerved inches from his knees. Its rider braked hard, one boot scraping stone. Ben staggered backward, clutching his book like a shield. “Scusa,” he blurted. The woman pulled off her helmet. Black curls escaped around a face already bright with mischief. “That,” she said, “was the horn.” “I’m sorry. I was reading.” “Che idea. Does the book say the pavement is a safe place?” “I thought it was a map.” “Maps are not shields, Inglese.” “I’m British.” “Good. Then let’s begin again. Get out of my delivery lane.” “Ben,” he offered. “Alessandra. And stop looking at the fountain as if it owes you money.” “It told me to put a coin in.” “It lies. It’s a Roman opinion.” “Is that a fact?” “It is now.” She killed the engine. “I don’t bite,” she said. “Before nine, anyway.” “I wasn’t—was that an invitation to breakfast?” She looked at him properly then. “I was reassuring you. Don’t get ambitious.” “Right. Sorry.” “You keep doing that.” “Doing what?” “Apologizing as if breathing badly is a criminal offense.” Ben laughed, startled by his own lack of embarrassment. “I’m on holiday.” “No,” Alessandra said, “you’re in Rome. Holiday is a guide with a broken strap and a man explaining the Roman alphabet.” She held out a spare helmet. “Put this on. I’m going to Trastevere.” “I have appointments.” “Dopo? Tomorrow’s problem.” “I could get lost.” “Good. I have excellent directions.” “Where are we going?” “That’s the beauty of it.” “Was that meant to reassure me?” “No.” On the back, he kept his elbows politely tucked in while she threaded through scooters, laundry, and streets best crossed on foot. He clutched her jacket. She laughed, and when they crested the bridge, Rome exploded below them in copper domes and honey-colored stone. “Not in the guidebook,” he shouted. “Exactly!” At a café near Campo de’ Fiori, she ordered two cappuccini and, while Ben was absorbed in the fountain’s symbolism, slipped a small brass key from a hook under the till into her jacket. It was a useless key, a useful secret, and entirely unasked for. Ben noticed nothing. At least, she hoped he hadn’t. By early afternoon, they had eaten cacio e pepe in Monti and cherries in Trastevere, tangled with Vespas in the Gianicolo traffic, and argued about whether the Pantheon’s “temple” label was dishonest. Ben hit his shin on a bollard and apologized to it. Alessandra watched the retreating scooter, delighted. “I like this Rome,” he said, breathless. “You’re not supposed to like it. You’re supposed to be awed.” “I can do both?” “Clearly.” The guidebook disappeared somewhere beneath his backpack. For once, he did not seem worried. At five o’clock, Alessandra announced they were going “somewhere the guidebook forgot”: a roof above a faded apartment block, entered by a locked service gate. “How do you have that key?” Ben asked. “Does it matter?” “It belongs to someone.” “He owes me a favor. It’s only a view.” “This is trespassing.” “Exactly. It’s a good one.” He followed her up. Laundry stirred overhead; the dome of San Pietro glowed above a city like an unfinished manuscript. “I could fall,” Ben said. “Then don’t.” “That isn’t remotely reassuring.” “It wasn’t meant to be.” She caught his sleeve. Her grip was quick. He looked at her hand, not the drop. “This isn’t in the guidebook.” “Good.” For months, he had organized his life around what belonged in books: archives, syllabuses, obligation’s neat arithmetic. Standing somewhere forbidden, he felt disturbingly happy. “Perhaps I could get used to this,” Ben said. Alessandra’s private smile briefly silenced him. “Careful. One gets rather good at it.” A thunderclap drowned Ben’s reply. The afternoon broke into rain, sudden and silver, drumming the rooftops. They ran for the yellow awning of a gelato shop, arriving soaked and laughing. Inside, the owner shouted, “Aspettate!” “Let them have shelter,” Ben said. “Or the ice will melt,” Alessandra replied. “It always does,” he said, watching her. She smiled and handed him the pistachio. “Sei gentile, English.” “Always.” “Clearly not always. It is your best quality and your worst decision.” Thunder rolled over the street. Her drenched curls clung to her neck. Ben pushed his glasses up; she reached across to wipe one smear with her thumb. The touch was brief. Neither stepped back. “So,” she murmured, “still glad you missed your appointments?” “Surprisingly, yes.” “Why?” “I’m still trying to determine that.” “Good. Rome is better with unanswered questions.” “Your country, not mine.” “Tonight, we share it.” At the curb, she pulled on her helmet and turned back. For a moment, the visor made her look dangerous again; then she smiled. “Phone number,” she said, scrawling it across his guidebook’s blank page. “Don’t call at nine. I’m working.” “How about tomorrow?” “Tomorrow isn’t a promise.” “But it isn’t a no.” “No.” Her smile sharpened. “It isn’t.” “Piazza Nomentana,” she added. “Eight o’clock.” “Why there?” “Because I haven’t decided where we’re going.” “You expect me to come?” “I expect you to be interesting. Try not to be late.” “Was that a threat or an invitation?” “It was a choice. I gave you an hour’s notice.” The scooter vanished into traffic. Ben remained beneath the awning, glasses fogged, guidebook against his chest. For once, he did not need to know what came next. He was already there, somehow, and he knew it.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical competence and largely succeeds in fulfilling the prompt's requirements. The author establishes two distinct characters with contrasting personalities - Alessandra's impulsive, mischievous energy versus Ben's polite, academic restraint - and maintains their voices consistently throughout. The Roman setting is well-integrated, moving naturally from tourist landmarks to more intimate, hidden spaces. The dialogue feels authentic and serves multiple purposes: revealing character, advancing the relationship, and providing humor. Exchanges like "Maps are not shields, Inglese" and "You keep doing that... Apologizing as if breathing badly is a criminal offense" efficiently establish Alessandra's sharp wit while showing Ben's endearing awkwardness. The banter has a natural rhythm that captures the cultural clash and growing attraction. The narrative structure works well, using short scenes connected by time markers that create momentum while allowing for character development. The author skillfully incorporates Alessandra's kleptomania through subtle actions (the brass key theft) rather than explicit exposition, showing restraint and trusting the reader. However, there are some weaknesses. The prose occasionally becomes overly literary in ways that feel forced - phrases like "water pretending not to be in a hurry" and "Rome exploded below them in copper domes and honey-colored stone" veer toward purple prose. Some metaphors feel strained, particularly "a city like an unfinished manuscript." The character development, while competent, follows somewhat predictable patterns. Ben's transformation from rigid academic to willing rule-breaker happens quickly, though the author does provide sufficient motivation through Alessandra's magnetic personality and his own dissatisfaction with routine. The ending strikes an appropriate note of ambiguity and possibility without forcing premature romantic resolution. The final image of Ben standing with his fogged glasses, no longer needing to know what comes next, effectively captures his transformation while maintaining believability. + Cozy sci-fi: The Last Outpost — Score: 82.2
Prompt:
Cozy sci-fi The Last Outpost Nettle (or Nets to her friends) bartends at The Last Outpost -- a lazy hub for miners and merchants in an asteroid belt on the Andromeda outer rim. Escaping from her past life, Nets found a home here at the Outpost. They have, thus far, tolerated Net's flaws which she tries to keep in equilibrium with her assortment of talents. Her evenings involve chatting with patrons, negotiating the drama, intrigue, problems & love lives of the diverse crowd that filter through the Outpost. Tonight is no different, at least, until a frazzled looking stranger, tentacled dreads askew, quietly plops down at the bar: "Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double." Write a chapter in this story. Establish conflict for narrative interest. Don't resolve the conflict within this chapter. Aim for about 60% dialogue. First person, present tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
“Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double.” The stranger hunches over the bar as though the airlock might swallow them if they straighten. Their coat is three sizes too large, patched at one elbow with insulation tape. Tentacled dreads trail over one shoulder, their tips uneven and singed. I reach beneath the counter for the bottle of Vega most customers order once, then regret. “That’ll be eight credits.” “Put it on my tab.” “You have a tab?” “Not yet. I was hoping to establish one under another name.” I pour two measures. The whisky trembles as the station’s gravity gives a small, mechanical shudder, climbing almost halfway up the glass before settling again. “First visits usually start with hello,” I say. “Hello. I need a favor, Nets.” “That’s two visits in one. Nearly a package deal.” I slide the glass across. The stranger studies it without touching it. Their fingers have the translucent edges of someone who works in vacuum. “Call me Tam,” they say. I wipe a ring from the counter, then another. The station’s late shift trickles through the Outpost in ones and twos: a freight pilot nursing tea, two merchants arguing about tariffs, a miner at the far table pretending not to listen. I like bartending. People arrive with their armor lowered, one drink at a time. Usually, the biggest trouble is a broken heart and an overdue tab. “I don’t run a favor economy,” I tell Tam. “I run a bar.” They place a battered copper token beside the glass. A nine-knot mark curls around its rim, with three lines struck through the center. My smile stays where it is, but something behind it goes careful. “Where did you get that?” “From someone who remembers the Harrow run.” “That was six years ago.” “Yes.” “And I was paid.” “You were underpaid,” Tam says. “And you left before finishing the job.” I set the bottle down too hard. The whisky leaps over the rim, catching itself in time. “I remember paying the hotel,” I say. “I remember the coffee. You made it too strong, and I complained all morning.” “That wasn’t tact.” “It was accurate.” For a moment, the noise of the station fills the space between us: ventilation, a distant drill, the soft clank of dishes in the kitchen. “I brought you here,” Tam says. “I was also the clerk who hired you.” My hands want to busy themselves. I straighten a rack of glasses that doesn’t need straightening. “Nell was another person’s name.” “She was your name,” Tam says. “You used it for three years.” “I don’t use it now.” “I’m counting on that.” They slide a second object onto the bar. It’s a memory core no larger than my thumb, smoky glass wrapped around a copper filament. No station inventory number. No shipping label. “I need this transmitted off-world,” Tam says. “Tonight.” “No.” “You haven’t heard what it is.” “That’s generally how I prefer my illegal cargo.” “It contains the colonists’ final testimony from the Harrow evacuation. The Combine ruled the messages inadmissible. This archive is admissible.” I look at the core. I look at the untouched whisky. “Why me?” “Because you can get through locked places, you know a dozen pilots who owe you favors, and the Combine revoked my license. Also, you care.” “That last one’s mostly true.” Tam leans closer. “I know what you carried, Nets. The red case. The launch authorization.” The room doesn’t change. The gravity doesn’t falter. Somehow everything does. “I carried an order,” I say. “Not a conscience.” “The order kept the evacuation shuttle on the freight spur for six hours. Two hundred and nine people were aboard when the pressure failed.” “I remember.” “I thought you might. That’s why I came.” I reach for the whisky, then stop myself. “You stole it from the Combine.” “I preserved it.” “You stole it from the Combine.” Tam’s mouth twists. “Those aren’t always different.” “No,” I agree. “They’re just easier to say in a bar.” I should end this there. I should pour them another drink, find them a room, and pretend curiosity isn’t another of my more expensive habits. Six years ago, I thought helping people meant carrying whatever they asked, wherever they asked, without looking inside the box. I learned different when someone else opened it. I tap the core with one fingernail. “How long do I have?” “Seven minutes to reach a ship. Eleven to upload the archive before the Combine challenges its authentication.” “So you need a miracle.” “I need you.” “That’s worse.” A chair creaks near the door. A suited figure has entered, pale armor gleaming beneath the bar’s warm lights. The black-and-silver crest of the Meridian Combine sits over their heart. The gravity pulses again. Every drink on the bar shivers. “We’re closed,” I say. “No,” the visitor says. “You’re inconvenient. Bring me the archive and the former courier registered as Nell, and the rest of your evening gets uncomplicated.” “I don’t know a Nell.” They raise a scanner. Its blue light hums across the room, pausing on each startled face. Tam lowers their hand beneath the bar. I place a coaster over the memory core. “Don’t scan my customers.” “The core is Combine property.” “Then don’t spill anything on my counter.” “Step away from it, barkeep.” “You have a name?” “Inspector Vey. And I know yours.” “Everyone does. I’m excellent at being memorable.” Vey sets a data wafer on the bar. A photograph appears above it: a younger woman with my eyes, standing beside a freight locker. The label reads **COURIER AUTHORIZATION: NELL**. Nell is a name I buried so thoroughly I sometimes pretend she was fictional. “That photo’s old,” I say. “You’ve hidden well,” Vey replies. “Not well enough.” Tam exhales. “This is your fault.” “Yes,” I say. “It usually is.” I slide the whisky bottle between us. The amber liquid sways inside the glass, stubbornly refusing to behave. “Here’s what happens next,” I tell them both. “Nobody moves, nobody threatens my bar, and whoever has the worst secret explains it before I do.” Vey’s scanner turns toward me. “Also,” I add, “nobody scans Dory. He’s paid through next rotation, and it would ruin my whole evening.” “I can pay mine,” Dory calls from his table. “But not the drink. I’ve seen what you pour strangers.” “That,” I say, pointing at him, “is loyalty.” Tam looks at the coaster hiding the archive. “What is it going to be, Nets?” I draw the core toward my palm but don’t lift it. Its filament ticks beneath the glass, faint as a watch counting down to something terrible. “I suppose,” I say, “we’d better find out.”

The author successfully maintains first-person present tense throughout and achieves approximately the requested 60% dialogue ratio. The 1000-word target is met, and crucially, conflict is established without resolution, as requested. The character work is particularly strong. Nets emerges as a compelling protagonist with a mysterious past, displaying wit, competence, and moral complexity. Her voice is consistent throughout - sardonic, observant, and protective of her establishment and patrons. Tam is effectively portrayed as desperate yet familiar with Nets' history, while Inspector Vey serves as an appropriately threatening antagonist. The dialogue feels natural and serves multiple purposes: advancing plot, revealing character, and building tension. The world-building is efficiently handled through subtle details - the gravity fluctuations, vacuum-scarred fingers, the mix of species and occupations. The setting feels lived-in and authentic without over-explanation. The prose is clean and purposeful, with effective use of sensory details like the whisky trembling in the glass during gravity shifts. The central conflict involving Nets' past as "Nell," the Harrow evacuation tragedy, and the stolen archive creates genuine moral complexity. The revelation that Nets unknowingly contributed to civilian deaths adds weight to her current dilemma. This backstory feels earned rather than convenient. However, some elements feel slightly predictable - the mysterious past catching up with the protagonist is a familiar trope, though it's executed well here. + Young adult drama: Gone South — Score: 83.4
Prompt:
Young adult drama Gone South Taylor is a 16 year old teen with a history of "concerning behavioural patterns" (or that's how the stupid smug school counsellor worded it on the phone call to Mom). It shouldn't be a surprise: When you live in a backwater town in Tennessee, your choices are: a. be mind-fuckingly bored, or b. invent some drama. Two days ago, Taylor came out to their family as trans. This disclosure was *not* in the category of invented drama -- it was, in fact, the real deal, and a long time coming. It didn't go well. The last 48 hours had been pure disaster. In a moment of desperate inspiration, Taylor had decided to get the hell out of dodge. And so an escape plan was hatched and executed within the space of 30 minutes. That was last night. Now Taylor was two states away, having been unceremoniously ejected from their hitched ride in downtown New Orleans. Write the next chapter in Taylor's story as they find their feet in this new environment. Tell the chapter over the course of their first day in New Orleans, in which Taylor meets another runaway with issues and secrets. Taylor navigates this new world, not knowing who to trust or what the dangers are. Write in Taylor's voice, and incorporate their internal monologue as they grapple with intense & conflicting emotions. Also incorporate dialogue with the interesting characters Taylor meets. First person, mixed tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Twelve percent.** I stare at my phone until the screen dims, as if I can bully twelve percent into becoming a hundred. I turn it facedown on the bench. The Mississippi shines brown and ugly below the levee. Nobody here is waiting to call my mother. That should feel like freedom. Instead, I feel like a stranger on the wrong side of a locked door. My duffel holds two hoodies, clean underwear, a toothbrush, and twenty-three dollars I’d saved for a concert. A place, not a future: that’s what New Orleans was supposed to be. No charger in sight. Two days ago, I told my family I’m trans. Yesterday, I left. My parents didn’t throw me out; I keep insisting on that, even when the story sounds worse in my own head. They were scared. They said things that landed like blows. I love them, and I hate that I can’t stop loving yesterday’s version of them while grieving who they might become. I feel terrible for wanting a world where my name is true and my parents are happy in it. Mostly, I feel tired. Free. Homesick enough to choke. I walk past St. Louis Cathedral, beneath balconies shedding paint like the city has given up on dignity. At eleven percent, I find the library’s only working bathroom. The woman at the desk points down a hall. “Family bathroom’s closed for cleaning,” she says. I almost say I understand. I don’t. I press my palm to the wall. It’s just a door. It’s just a room. I turn on the faucet, watch the water disappear, and whisper, “Still here. Still me.” I am somebody’s kid. I am a runaway. I am terrified, and I am still here. Both. All of it. In the reading room, a boy with a bleached buzz cut and a jacket two sizes too big watches the doors. He looks about my age, which means seventeen or twenty—the sort of math nobody gets right. “You see anybody with a red bag?” he asks. “Red bag?” “Canvas. He’s got my phone.” I should leave. I should absolutely, definitely leave. Instead, I pick up my backpack. “Don’t,” the boy says. “He’s already seen me.” Great. So I’m either involved in theft or mistaken for an accomplice. Perfect morning. The doors open. The man in the red canvas bag comes in, scans the room, and sits where he can watch both exits. My stomach drops. The boy notices. “His name’s Arthur,” he whispers. “And he’s scared of me, not the other way around.” “Is that supposed to reassure me?” “No. It’s supposed to keep you from making a stupid decision.” I hate him immediately. That is, I hate how much I recognize the warning. I walk toward the doors. Arthur’s eyes follow me. I used to be invisible. Apparently that came with an expiration date. “Don’t go out there,” the boy calls. I turn. “What do you suggest? Steal a phone back?” He winces. “I didn’t take it. I found it.” “That’s not remotely better.” “No,” he agrees. “But it’s a start.” Arthur gets up. “Remy,” the boy says, and his voice cracks. He nods toward the courtyard. I don’t follow. Except I do. Outside, I point at the NO SMOKING sign. Remy sighs like the sign has disappointed him personally. “Fine. I’m trying to be approachable.” “I don’t care if you’re approachable. I care if you’re honest.” “Those are often the same thing.” “Usually?” He studies me. “No last name. The phone was already in my bag when I found it. Okay?” I should tell Arthur. I should tell him I don’t know this boy, except I know exactly what it feels like to have a secret make your shoulders ache. “For now,” I say. “That’s what worries me.” By the time we leave, I’m at nine percent, and my duffel feels packed with bad decisions. We walk toward the river, then away from it. I tell myself I’m going to the bus station. The truth is less dignified: Remy is walking, and I don’t want to be alone. “You’re following me,” he says. “No.” “You keep looking over your shoulder.” “I’ve got reasons.” “Good ones?” “I left home forty-eight hours ago.” He considers this. “That’s a start.” At the next red light, I ask where he’s running from. “Would you believe me if I said the weather?” “No.” “Good answer. I don’t know. I know I’m not going back.” He scuffs his shoe on the pavement. “I stole the wallet in my bag. I needed bus money. The phone was already gone when I found it. And now Arthur thinks I’m dangerous, and I think Arthur might be right.” The light changes. Neither of us moves. “You don’t know that,” I say. “No. But I know what it feels like when somebody decides you’re the villain before you’ve finished being a person.” We cross. His face isn’t proud. He isn’t sorry enough, either. Just calculation, trying to fit the damage into a shape he can carry. “Can I trust you?” He doesn’t pretend to be offended. “Absolutely not.” It’s the most honest answer he’s given me. “Don’t look at me like I’m already a bad movie,” Remy says. “I know I’m not the hero.” “Neither do I.” Instead of being terrified, I feel less alone: inconvenient, probably dangerous. I want somebody worth trusting. Worse, I might be one. We reach the bus station as the sky goes orange. Three percent. Remy watches the doors. The attendant notices us hovering by her desk. “You two need help?” I open my mouth. What comes out is, “I don’t know.” It’s true. I don’t want to go home. I don’t want to disappear. I want somewhere safe to sleep, someone who won’t make me feel like a diagnosis, and enough courage to ask for one thing at a time. Remy looks at me. I look at him. “Yes,” I say. “We need help.” Three percent isn’t much. It’s enough to keep asking.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and emotional authenticity in portraying a transgender teen runaway's first day in New Orleans. The writing successfully captures Taylor's voice through a mix of vulnerability, defiance, and sharp observation that feels genuinely adolescent without being patronizing. The characterization is particularly strong. Taylor emerges as a complex protagonist - neither purely victim nor hero, but someone making difficult choices with limited options. The internal monologue effectively conveys the conflicting emotions of someone who chose to leave rather than being thrown out, creating nuanced guilt and grief. Remy is equally well-developed, avoiding the trap of being either romanticized or demonized as a fellow runaway with moral ambiguity. The prose style is confident and controlled, with effective use of concrete details (the phone battery percentage, specific dollar amounts, physical descriptions of New Orleans) that ground the narrative in reality. The dialogue feels natural and serves character development well, particularly Remy's honest admission that Taylor shouldn't trust him. The pacing moves effectively through Taylor's first day, building tension through the library encounter and resolving with a moment of connection that feels earned rather than forced. The ending strikes an appropriate balance - offering hope without suggesting Taylor's problems are solved. Some minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the internal monologue becomes slightly overwrought, and a few instances where the prose edges toward being too polished for a teen narrator. The plot structure, while solid, follows somewhat predictable beats for a runaway narrative. The piece successfully adheres to most prompt requirements, though it could have pushed further into exploring the specific dangers and atmosphere of New Orleans as a setting. The emotional complexity and authentic voice largely overcome these minor shortcomings. + Dystopic-comedy: My Apocalypse Buddy — Score: 84.5
Prompt:
My Apocalypse Buddy Write a wry, dry short story of survival and adventure loosely in the style of Terry Pratchett, set in the post-technological collapse world. The story begins with the pair deliberating their predicament and intent for the day's mission, details the ways in which the mission inevitably goes sideways, and returns them to home base in multiple ways, worse for wear. [characters] - the animo-tronic stuffed koala, Chewy, from some long forgotten before time - midas, our hapless protagonist, who has a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# My Apocalypse Buddy The plan for the day was to get antibiotics from Rowland’s Pharmacy, four miles north, and return before dark. It was a good plan. It had survived being spoken aloud and was therefore statistically doomed. Midas had named himself after a legendary example of poor judgment. He had no gift for turning things into gold, but possessed a remarkable talent for turning useful objects into hazards at the exact moment everybody had begun to rely on them. He was currently lying on a trolley in the library’s second-floor reading room, holding a jar of boiled water against his infected forearm. It had been infected since he had used a shopping trolley as an improvised splint. The trolley had also acquired a wheel that turned sideways, which made the splint necessary in the first place. Their headquarters was the library because it had defensible windows, excellent walls, and books containing several hundred years of accumulated expertise, none of it any use whatsoever for treating infection. Chewy sat beside him on the trolley. Chewy was an animatronic koala who had survived the end of the technological world by being too badly designed to qualify as technology. His batteries had died decades ago, but his voice box, clockwork joints, and capacity for expressing disappointment still worked. Midas had found him in a ransacked bedroom, beneath a sign reading WELCOME, LITTLE FRIEND, which had not been followed by the best possible outcome. His eyes flickered green when relieved, yellow when uneasy, red when alarmed, and blue when he was frightened but trying to look otherwise. At present they were yellow. “We need the antibiotics,” Midas said. “I am concerned about the antibiotics,” said Chewy. “That’s not quite—” “Chewy, do not worry.” Chewy’s eyes immediately flickered blue. Midas took this as a review of his performance. The library’s largest surviving map showed three possible routes north. There was the main road, the river path, and the old railway bridge. The bridge had been washed out. The river path was flooded. The main road was technically a main road, which meant that it had been designed to carry a great deal of traffic and was now carrying only bicycles, wild dogs, and increasingly suspicious livestock. “We go along the main road,” Midas said. “We stay together. We don’t stop for anything that looks interesting. We get the medicine and come straight back.” Chewy’s eyes went yellow again. “You’re worried about the plan.” “I’m worried that you’ve described the plan with excessive confidence.” “There’s a difference.” “Yes,” said Chewy. “Usually it involves someone being wrong.” They set off shortly afterward. Midas carried Chewy inside his jacket, a position Chewy described as warm, dark, and anatomically inconvenient. Midas told him it was only a few miles. Chewy replied that, in his experience, several things Midas had said had eventually turned out to be more than a few miles, including “I’ll just check this noise” and “I’ve got a clever idea.” The main road was not impassable. It was merely impassable in the manner of a road that had become more of a suggestion. They found Rowland’s Pharmacy beyond a supermarket whose automatic doors continued opening and closing at intervals, as if the building were greeting someone important. Inside, the shelves had been stripped, the floor was gritty, and a handwritten sign informed them that prescriptions were no longer accepted because the pharmacist was no longer alive. “He did leave a note,” Chewy said. “Of course he did. People always leave a note explaining how the world has ended.” It was not a particularly helpful note. Midas searched behind the counter while Cheyw kept watch through the grimy window. Antibiotics, if any remained, would be in the storeroom. Midas found it locked. He considered the door, the crowbar beside it, and the section of ceiling that seemed to be holding up the door by personal conviction. Then he noticed a serving hatch. It was eighteen inches high. “He must have been very ill,” Midas said. “You are not going to climb through that.” “I could climb through that.” “You have an infected arm.” “I can climb through it slowly.” Chewy’s eyes flickered red, an emotion usually associated with Midas explaining what he intended to do next. Fortunately for everyone, the hatch was merely ugly. It took Midas twenty minutes to get through it and cost him most of the remaining strength in his arm. The storeroom was dark, hot, and full of cardboard. A distant motor whirred. “What was that?” Midas asked. “Nothing,” said Chewy. “It sounded like something.” “It sounded like something starting. This is not the reassurance you imagine.” A robot came out from behind a shelving unit. It was a floor-cleaning machine, round, white, and equipped with a brush beneath it that had clearly spent years thinking about violence. A little display panel showed its remaining charge at three percent. It had survived the apocalypse by being extremely good at its job and completely unable to understand the concept of retirement. Chewy’s eyes flickered blue. “Do not move,” he said. “I wasn’t going to.” “You were thinking about it.” Midas backed away. The robot advanced. Its brush began spinning. “I know,” said Chewy, “that you are now trying to think of a way to stop a floor-cleaning machine.” “I have one.” “I’m sure you do.” “It has a battery cover.” “Then that is one for you and one for the charge indicator.” Midas opened the cover with the loose end of his belt. The robot reversed, emitted a noise of great mechanical disappointment, and came at him again. Chewy shouted, “EXCUSE ME!” at maximum volume. The robot accelerated. “Don’t shout at it!” “IT IS MY BEST REMAINING FEATURE!” Midas seized a box of painkillers, kicked a bucket under the robot, and fled through the storeroom hatch. The bucket caught the brush. The robot spun in place, emitting a continuous howl that brought three dogs to the pharmacy door. The first homeward attempt was a shopping trolley. Midas put the antibiotic bottle inside his jacket, placed Chewy in the basket, and pushed. The trolley behaved well for almost thirty yards. Then it encountered a pothole, jumped sideways, and deposited both of them into a compost heap. Midas lay in the compost, breathing through his teeth. Cheyw lay on top of him, one ear folded over his face. “That was a bad way home,” Chewy said. “I’m aware.” “The second way home was a dog.” It was not the sort of dog people usually chose for company. It was enormous, yellow, and extremely enthusiastic. It had apparently decided that Midas and Chewy required escorting, and it expressed this opinion by placing one hand in Midas’s good sleeve and beginning to pull. Midas did not resist. He had reached the point in the day where the principle of conservation of energy was more important than the principle of personal dignity. The dog dragged them along the pavement for half a mile. Chewy hung from the basket with one arm wrapped around Midas’s neck and the other flapping in the air. “Do not let it eat me,” Chewy said. “It isn’t going to eat you.” “It has considered it.” “It hasn’t.” “I have seen its face,” said Chewy. “Its face is a complicated document.” At a broken section of pavement, the dog stopped. It was distracted by a discarded sandwich. Midas and Chewy continued the journey by foot. The third way home was therefore mostly walking. Midas leaned on a wall. Cheyw leaned on Midas. The dog went off to investigate something in a garden, taking the shopping trolley with it. “It was a good dog,” Midas said. “It is a good dog,” said Chewy. “It has simply mistaken us for rubbish.” They reached the library an hour after dark. Midas’s arm was worse. His trousers had acquired a convincing theory of the entire lower leg. Chewy’s stuffing was escaping from a seam in his back, and his left foot was pointing toward the middle of next week. His voice box clicked, produced a brief fragment of an announcement about the importance of dental hygiene, and fell silent. Midas carried him up the fire escape. This was the fourth way home, although nobody was in a condition to count. They collapsed into the reading room. Midas set the antibiotics on the table. Cheyw sat beside them with his remaining foot sticking out at an ambitious angle. “We got the medicine,” Midas said. “We got a great many things,” Chewy replied. “A small number of them were medicine.” Migas looked at the bottle. Then he looked at the room: the mud, the scattered bandages, the shopping trolley in the corner, the trail of stuffing leading toward the stairs. He began to laugh, and then stopped, because laughing hurt. “Tomorrow,” he said, “we’re taking the river path.” Chewy’s eyes flickered yellow. “Good,” he said, as Midas’s eyes closed. “I was worried you’d choose the main road again.” His own eyes settled to a steady green. Not because everything was fine, but because at least the two of them were home.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates a strong grasp of Terry Pratchett's distinctive style, capturing his dry wit, observational humor, and philosophical undertones effectively. The author successfully creates a post-apocalyptic world that feels both bleak and absurdly comedic, maintaining the required tone throughout. The characterization is particularly well-executed. Midas is established as a genuinely hapless protagonist whose self-awareness about his poor judgment creates both humor and pathos. His naming himself after a figure of poor judgment is a clever touch that establishes character efficiently. Chewy, the animatronic koala, serves as an excellent foil - his color-coded emotional states and dry observations provide consistent humor while avoiding the trap of being merely a comic relief device. The dialogue captures Pratchett's rhythm well, with exchanges that feel natural while maintaining the author's distinctive voice. The conversations between Midas and Chewy have genuine chemistry, and their banter reveals character while advancing the plot. Lines like "I'm worried that you've described the plan with excessive confidence" perfectly capture the dry, understated humor of the source material. The plot structure adheres closely to the prompt requirements - beginning with deliberation, showing how the mission goes sideways, and ending with their return home "worse for wear." The escalating series of mishaps (the robot, the trolley, the dog) creates good comedic momentum without feeling forced. The prose demonstrates genuine elegance in places, with memorable phrases like "a road that had become more of a suggestion" and "His face is a complicated document." The author shows restraint in avoiding purple prose while maintaining vivid imagery. However, there are some weaknesses. The pacing occasionally feels rushed, particularly in the pharmacy sequence where the robot encounter could have been developed more fully. Some transitions between scenes feel abrupt, and certain comedic beats could have been given more space to breathe. The ending strikes an appropriate balance - they succeed in their mission but at considerable cost, which feels earned rather than artificially positive. The final exchange about taking the river path tomorrow provides a satisfying circular structure while maintaining the characters' established dynamic. The piece successfully avoids common pitfalls like overwrought emotion or unearned character transformations. The humor emerges naturally from character and situation rather than being forced, and the world-building feels consistent and believable within its absurdist framework. + Romance: Love in the Limelight — Score: 83.2
Prompt:
Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write one scene within a larger story set in Wales. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. The scene takes us through the characters meeting in this odd circumstance. Over the course of the scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Write the actor as somewhat of a rogue with a fragile ego, which needs to be fed by having everyone like him. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor's charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. 1000 words.
Model Output:
### Cardiff, Thursday, 5.42 p.m. The bell above the door gave a resigned jingle as a tall man in a baseball cap and an unnecessarily expensive coat slipped inside. He shut the door, pressed his back against it, and let out a breath. “You can breathe again,” said the woman behind the counter. He looked up. Red hair escaped beneath the cap; his eyes were pale, clever, and much too famous. “I was hoping you’d say that.” “Were you?” “I was hoping you’d say anything. I’ve had a difficult journey.” Gwen, who owned the bookshop and had spent the last twelve years reading difficult books at difficult hours, set down her receipt stamp. “Rhys Vale,” she said. “Guilty.” “You’re dripping on my floor.” “There’s something heroic about that.” “There really isn’t.” Outside, a camera lens strained towards them. The man glanced towards the rain-streaked window. “Could you—” “No.” “You didn’t even hear the question.” “You were going to ask me to hide you.” “I was going to ask if you had a back room.” “I have a back room. You can’t go in it.” “I could bribe you.” “I could evict you. That’s cheaper.” He laughed, visibly delighted. Gwen braced herself for the performance. It was probably easier to resist a famous actor when you saw the exact moment he decided to become charming. He removed the cap, shook rain from his hair, and smiled at her. “You always this welcoming, or is it a Thursday thing?” “It’s raining.” “That explains the weather, not the hostility.” “I try to make a favourable impression on as many people as possible.” “So you do like me.” “I said *try*.” His phone buzzed against his thigh. He ignored it. “Your shop is lovely.” “Don’t.” “Don’t what?” “Don’t be complimentary. I’m vulnerable. It’s all I have.” “That sounded rehearsed.” “It has been.” His smile shifted, briefly genuine. “My manager says I do that when I’m frightened.” Gwen’s eyes flicked to the window. A long lens had appeared beside the first. “Your manager is right,” she said. “The photographers are still there.” “Then I’ll stay.” “In the doorway?” “In the doorway, if it helps.” “It doesn’t.” He glanced around the shop: the crooked shelves, the handwritten recommendations, the Welsh-language novels beside the English ones. “Can you read Welsh?” he asked. “Can you?” “Enough.” “Enough to say *cariad*?” “I can say it very attractively.” “Wrongly, then.” He grinned at her. She did not grin back, but something flickered behind her careful expression. “*Cariad, cariad*,” he tried. “Not quite.” “Your version is better.” “Of course it is. I had a childhood in it. You had an accent lesson with a man shouting numbers in a market.” “I also had eleven years of Welsh schooling.” “That explains the confidence, not the pronunciation.” His phone buzzed again. This time he looked at the screen. *CAR PICKUP 7 A.M. CONFIRM SCHEDULE.* “My life has an understudy,” he said. “Nothing to do with me?” “Not unless you have strong opinions about horses.” “I only have strong opinions about people who interrupt inventory.” “I’ll make this quick. I don’t want to get you in trouble.” “I’m already in trouble. You’ve been here six minutes.” “I can leave.” “No.” She seemed surprised by herself. “You can sit. I’ve decided.” “Should I be charmed?” “You should be grateful. I’m not often this merciful.” She moved towards the little coffee machine. He watched her fill the kettle. “Strong coffee,” he said. “Milk, no sugar.” “I know.” “You do?” “I watched you drink half a cup at the café in the Castle Arcade this morning.” “You followed me?” “You went past the same window three times. It seemed less like following and more like indecision.” “I was making sure they’d lost me.” “You put your cap on backwards, went into a bookshop, and asked the owner where the nearest underground car park was. I offered directions. You left before I finished.” “So you noticed me.” “I notice impatience. There was a lot of it in you.” He laughed. “That may be the nicest thing anyone’s said to me this week.” “It wasn’t a compliment.” “I’m choosing to take it as one.” “I think that’s the point.” She brought him the coffee. Their fingers brushed when he took it. He didn’t withdraw immediately. Neither did she. Then she withdrew, and the moment folded itself away. “You’re not actually immune, are you?” he said quietly. “I beg your pardon?” “It’s all right. I was stupid.” “I have no idea what you’re talking about.” “You keep looking at me as if you don’t know what to do with me.” “I know exactly what to do with you. Put you in that chair by the door. The photographers can see it when they come in.” “Are they leaving?” “Not yet.” “So that strategy has flaws.” “Most of mine do.” He looked down at his coffee. Outside, Cardiff disappeared into silver rain. “They think I’m a great actor,” he said. “Everyone wants the version of me they can recognise. They like the handsome idiot from the film, or the charming fool in the interviews. I keep offering them that man because he works.” “And does he?” “He leaves before anyone sees him properly.” Gwen studied him. For once, she offered no quick reply. “Perhaps that’s why you keep asking whether people like you,” she said. “Most people do.” “No. Most people are polite.” “That sounds dangerously like honesty.” “Rain does that to a place.” “Does it also explain why you haven’t asked me to leave?” “Because you bought a coffee.” “It was one pound twenty.” “Exactly. I’m making excellent money.” He smiled, but she had found the bruise beneath it. “So I’m what?” he asked. “A customer?” “An expensive way to pass the time.” “Is that what this is?” “At the moment, yes.” “No, I mean—” He turned the cup in his hands. “I can do the charming thing. Usually, I do it before I get here. It’s rather effective.” “I know.” “You do?” “I’ve seen your interviews.” “And?” “And you do it there too.” “Was I awful?” “Perfectly adequate. You looked at everyone as if you were waiting for the right person to walk into the room.” “And they never do?” “They interrupt too quickly.” He glanced up. This time his smile did not reach the performance. Gwen looked away first. “You should go,” she said, though she did not move towards the door. “Your advice is as charming as your welcome.” “I’m Welsh. We say what we mean.” “No, you certainly don’t.” “Ask me something difficult instead.” He lifted the cup. “What do you think I want?” “That I admire you.” “I’d like to be liked.” “I know.” “No, you don’t.” Her expression changed. “Yes,” she said. “I do. That’s rather inconvenient.” The cameras clicked outside. He was quiet for a moment. “Can I buy you a drink?” he asked. “Somewhere without photographers?” “No.” “Much worse coffee?” “I just made you some.” “I liked the coffee.” “And?” “The company. Mostly the company.” “I can tolerate the company.” “Is that an invitation?” “It’s an observation. Don’t get excited.” “I never do.” “You are.” “Charming?” “Impossible.” “I usually have a closing date for impossible.” “I close at six.” “It’s seven past.” “Then you should have asked before six.” He glanced at the shelves between them, at the narrow space crowded with other people’s private lives. “I don’t know how to do this without an audience,” he admitted. “Perhaps don’t do it.” “That’s a novel concept.” “It’s usually a good one.” “No, I mean—” He pushed his untouched coffee towards her. “I think you might be my favourite person today.” “Today?” “I met another actor this morning. He was very impressive. Wanted a detailed account of my feelings.” “I hope you gave him one.” “Not the right details.” “Perhaps you’ll find them in a book.” “Do you have one in mind?” “I do, actually. There’s a Welsh thriller with a completely insufferable hero. A man who mistakes being admired for being liked.” “I think I know him.” “I wonder. The back cover says he learns humility.” “Does he?” “No. But there’s a sequel.” “I’ll take it.” “You won’t like it.” “I liked your company. I’ve made my decision.” For the first time, Gwen’s careful defences failed to conceal the small, helpless pleasure crossing her face. She looked down at her ink-stained fingers. “Go home, Rhys Vale.” “All right.” “And stop enjoying this.” “Which part?” “Any of it.” He picked up a battered Welsh-language thriller from beside the till. “For the paperback,” he said. “It’s not for sale.” “I’ll give you my signature.” “I don’t want your signature.” “I’ll stay and discuss the insufferable hero.” She looked at the book, then at him. “Stay until the rain stops,” she said. “Then go home.” “All right.” “And it’s not an invitation.” “Of course not.” “It’s a retail decision.” “I understand.” “You don’t.” “No,” he said softly. “I don’t.” For once, he wasn’t waiting for someone else to tell him.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and adherence to the prompt requirements. The author successfully creates the requested Welsh setting, establishes the meet-cute scenario with paparazzi pursuit, and develops both characters according to their specified archetypes. The dialogue-driven approach works well, with each character maintaining distinct voices throughout. The characterization is particularly effective. Rhys Vale emerges as genuinely charming yet insecure, his need for validation clearly driving his behavior. His charm offensive visibly shifts when met with resistance, revealing vulnerability beneath the performance. Gwen is equally well-drawn - her sharp wit and apparent immunity to his charm masking her growing attraction. The author skillfully shows her internal conflict through small moments like the finger-brush scene and her final capitulation. The dialogue crackles with wit and subtext. Lines like "I try to make a favourable impression on as many people as possible" / "So you do like me" / "I said *try*" demonstrate sharp comedic timing while advancing character development. The Welsh cultural elements feel authentic rather than forced, particularly in the language exchange about "cariad." The pacing builds tension effectively through their verbal sparring, with moments of genuine connection breaking through the banter. The author avoids overwrought emotional declarations, instead letting attraction develop through resistance and small revelations. Rhys's admission "I don't know how to do this without an audience" feels earned rather than forced. However, some elements feel slightly predictable - the basic dynamic of charming celebrity meeting resistant local follows familiar romance patterns. The ending, while sweet, doesn't surprise. Some descriptions occasionally veer toward the precious ("the moment folded itself away"), though this remains restrained overall. The prose flows naturally with good rhythm and variety in sentence structure. The author demonstrates control over tone, maintaining romantic tension without becoming saccharine. The piece engages throughout, building to a satisfying if gentle conclusion that feels appropriate for a single scene within a larger work.
