+ Gothic-fantasy-humour: Court of the Dreaming — Score: 82.8
Prompt:
Court of the Dreaming: Territorial Dream Dispute. Write a dark fantasy scene with comedic elements set in the Courts of Dream where a case is being heard to determine ownership of a contested dreamscape. Mora, the Slavic nightmare spirit who sits on sleepers' chests causing paralysis and terror, has recently invaded and subverted a carefully crafted recurring dream of a schoolboy, Max. The dream originally featured the boy lying in a field of wildflowers with his crush, always culminating in a muddled almost-kiss and a pleasant confusion of emotions. This dream was the meticulous work of "First Love" (a rosy-cheeked, slightly bashful entity who crafts formative romantic experiences). However, Mora has recently infiltrated the dreamscape, transforming the scene so that when the girl playfully mounts the boy, she morphs into a terrifying yet somehow still confusingly attractive vision who proceeds to sit on his chest and feed on his breath. Mora's defense largely consists of the practical argument that "a girl's gotta eat too, you know?" Write this scene as it unfolds in the courtroom of the Dreaming, with Dream's demeanour, typically impenetrable, betraying a sense of irritation at having to adjudicate such matters. The comedy should derive from the farcical situation, familiar elements of courtroom drama intersecting with the fantastical world of the Dreaming, and the droll portrayal of the characters and their interactions. The humor should be dark and understated throughout. Dream is tempted to some mischief in the resolution of the case. Use descriptives sparingly when setting scene. Write for readability & engagement. 1000 words.
Model Output:
A single, giant hourglass stood in the centre of the courtroom, dripping shimmering sand. Dream sat in judgment above it, looking like a monarch who had been asked to mediate between two headaches. Before him, First Love stood behind a lectern, rosy-cheeked and clutching her dream as a shopkeeper might clutch proof of ownership. Mora occupied the dock with the ease of a landlord awaiting an argument. “Your Honour,” said First Love, “I made this dream. Meadow, flowers, harmless longing, one carefully managed almost-kiss. It is the work of a lifetime, although the lifetime is rather short.” She offered the court a printed scene no larger than a school photograph. Max lay in the grass, his crush bending towards him. Her smile was lovely. The almost-kiss had been annotated in twelve coloured pencils, three apparently chewed. “I object,” said Mora. First Love objected to the objection. Dream looked between them. “The night dreams are in question, or have you brought me a scrapbook?” “The night dreams,” Mora said. “I have occupied the meadow. The boy is still there, though now he has company.” “She has subverted the emotional structure,” said First Love, with the dignity of someone discovering her wheelbarrow had been stolen. “He was meant to feel beautifully confused. Now he is being smothered by a beautiful nightmare.” “I saw no smothering,” said Mora. “I saw excellent ventilation.” First Love turned pink. “The girl was meant to remain herself. Instead, she has been given teeth, muscle, and an appetite.” “She kept the part that attracts him,” Mora said. “That seemed rude to spoil.” “A girl’s gotta eat too, you know?” she added. “A dream is not a free pantry. I merely sat down. The meadow was full of flowers, the boy was full of air, and neither was using the other for anything useful. I improved the evening.” Dream’s face betrayed nothing. This was how everyone knew he was irritated. He could end a kingdom with a raised eyebrow; here he was being made to adjudicate a boy’s breathing. The hourglass dripped. One grain climbed briefly upwards, then continued downwards as though it had reconsidered. “Entered a dream already in use?” Dream asked. “Entered a sleeping boy,” said Mora. “Found the meadow. Found the girl. Sat down.” “That is trespass.” “That is dinner.” First Love’s blush deepened. “I do not eat sleepers. I give them something to look forward to.” Mora’s smile showed one fang. “That is a claim to authority. I am the one with the fangs.” “You are also eating my air.” “Air is the most intimate thing a sleeper has.” Her practicality was hard to deny, especially to a sleeper. First Love held out her copy of the dream. “Her face kept changing. From a crush to a horror, and back again with interest. He was not to be frightened of her. He was to wonder whether she might, perhaps, kiss him. I was giving him room to wonder.” Mora nodded. “I removed the room. Now he wonders whether he will wake up. Both are memorable.” “Only one of them is an emotional education.” “I also charge less than an emotional education.” Dream turned a page in a ledger. The ledger whispered that it would rather not. “Max,” said Dream. “Come forward.” The boy appeared in the witness box, school uniform, bare feet, blinking within the green of his own meadow. His breathing was shallow. Daisies hovered above his chest, looking concerned. “Do you consent to Mora’s use of your dream?” Max glanced at her. “I thought we were talking about flowers.” “We are now.” “She sits on me,” Max said. “She turns into something with too many eyes, but the girl is still there. Sort of. She steals my breath. The flowers keep swaying. I don’t think I can move any more. I think I may be dreaming about being unable to move.” Mora said, “That is not accurate.” “Can I move?” “Not at present.” Dream’s expression remained perfect. His patience had entered its final stage, the one marked on maps by small drawings of gallows. First Love said, “Your Honour, the dream was made for the first stirring of feeling. I made it gentle. I made it safe.” “And I made it interesting,” said Mora. “By making him afraid.” “By making him remember her.” Dream regarded them both. “Who owns the meadow?” “The dream remains First Love’s work,” Dream said. “The meadow is hers. Mora may share the boy’s sleep with you, but the girl remains a girl. Find your supper in his nightmares instead.” First Love looked relieved. Mora looked less so. Mora said, “There is no point in a girl unless she has an appetite.” “Then let her have a hunger for the school dance,” said Dream. “On Friday, she will ask him. He will say no. On Saturday, she will ask again. On Sunday, he will still be thinking about Friday. The interruption will be educational.” Mischief stirred behind Dream’s gaze. Dream was having a rather lovely time. Mora stared at him. “You are joking.” Dream’s face did not move. “I am Dream. I am not joking. I am occasionally whimsical about Tuesdays.” He turned another ledger page. The whispering stopped. “And the night after the dance, you will explain quadratic equations to him,” he said. “One hundred nights. No eating. No interruptions.” Mora’s expression became a study in betrayal. “I am a terror of the night.” “You are also a guest. And the boy has mathematics.” First Love’s relief had returned, now accompanied by a smile that Dream pretended not to see. He closed the ledger, with rather more satisfaction than the sentence warranted. “The ruling is entered. Max returns to his bed. First Love restores her meadow. Mora leaves the flowers standing.” “And the daisies?” Mora asked. “Max was fond of the daisies.” Max vanished. First Love and the audience withdrew. Mora remained in the dock for one final appeal. “Your Honour,” she said, “I have never done sums.” Dream looked at her with the courteous blankness of a monarch contemplating an unnecessary cruelty. “No,” he said. “You have until tomorrow to become acquainted.”
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece successfully captures the essence of a Sandman-style courtroom drama with dark comedic elements. The author demonstrates strong adherence to the prompt's requirements, creating a believable Court of Dreams setting where supernatural entities dispute territorial rights over a mortal's dreamscape. The characterizations are particularly well-executed. Dream maintains his canonical imperious detachment while betraying subtle irritation at having to adjudicate such mundane matters. First Love embodies earnest propriety with her "rosy-cheeked" demeanor and protective stance over her carefully crafted romantic dream. Mora is delightfully pragmatic and unapologetic, delivering lines like "a girl's gotta eat too" with perfect comedic timing. The dialogue carries the piece effectively, with each character maintaining a distinct voice. Dream's formal, slightly archaic speech patterns contrast nicely with Mora's blunt practicality and First Love's flustered propriety. The exchanges feel natural while serving both comedic and plot purposes. The dark humor emerges organically from the situation rather than feeling forced. The juxtaposition of supernatural entities arguing over a teenage boy's romantic dreams using legal terminology creates inherent comedy. Lines like "I saw no smothering, I saw excellent ventilation" demonstrate the author's skill at understated humor. The prose style is appropriately spare, following the instruction to use descriptives sparingly. Sentences like "Dream sat in judgment above it, looking like a monarch who had been asked to mediate between two headaches" are economical yet evocative. The writing maintains good pacing and readability throughout. Dream's mischievous resolution feels earned and character-appropriate. Forcing Mora to teach mathematics as punishment shows both his sense of justice and his capacity for creative cruelty, while the final exchange about her inexperience with sums provides a satisfying comedic conclusion. The piece maintains tonal consistency throughout, balancing the fantastical elements with recognizable courtroom dynamics. The author successfully creates an engaging narrative that feels both otherworldly and grounded in familiar human experiences. Minor weaknesses include some moments where the comedy could be sharper, and occasionally the dialogue attribution could be cleaner. However, these are minor issues in an otherwise well-crafted piece that successfully fulfills the prompt's requirements. + Fanfic-crossover: Blood Moon — Score: 80.0
Prompt:
Blood Moon Alucard & Yennefer Write a story where Alucard (Hellsing) encounters Yennefer (The Witcher) in medieval Europe. Yennefer's magical abilities intrigue the vampire, while she's both repulsed and fascinated by his monstrous nature. Their power dynamic shifts constantly as they circle each other, neither willing to show weakness first. **Alucard (Hellsing)** Alucard is an ancient, immensely powerful vampire who works for the Hellsing Organization. He can regenerate from almost any wound and shape-shift at will. He's sadistic, arrogant, and takes pleasure in toying with his enemies before killing them. Despite being a monster, he despises weak vampires who can't accept their nature. He wears a distinctive red coat, wide-brimmed hat, and orange sunglasses. He uses massive handguns loaded with silver bullets. He seeks worthy opponents who can challenge him and potentially end his immortal existence. Famous quote: "The bird of Hermes is my name, eating my wings to make me tame." **Yennefer of Vengerberg (The Witcher)** Yennefer is a powerful sorceress who magically altered her appearance to hide her congenital hunchback. She's ambitious, stubborn, and manipulative when necessary. She has violet eyes and smells of lilac and gooseberries. Despite her cold exterior, she desperately wants to reverse her infertility caused by magical transformation. She's centuries old but appears young. She's politically savvy and refuses to be underestimated. She has a sarcastic sense of humor and little patience for fools. Though she rarely shows it, she's capable of deep love and loyalty. Famous quote: "I'm not sweet and I'm not a maiden in distress in need of saving." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Blood Moon The blood moon stains the clouds above the village, turning their undersides the color of old wounds. At the gates, a broken cart wheel lies in the mud, its axle snapped clean. One end points toward the empty road; the other disappears beneath the wheel’s shattered rim. Yennefer of Vengerberg stops beside it. No tracks leave the village. None return. The iron hinges of the gate have been twisted apart, and the watchman’s spear rests against the wall where he apparently dropped it. She draws a thin blade from her boot and tests the air. No magic. No blood. Only the iron smell of recent violence. Beyond the gates, three houses stand with their doors open. Market stalls lie overturned in the market square. A dog moves between them, nosing at something beneath a fallen awning, too frightened to bark. The village has emptied in haste. Its people have heard a legend Yennefer followed herself: the saint’s well in the village chapel grants impossible gifts. To her, that means a child. To others, it means eternal life. She sheathes the blade and walks into the square. On the mounting stone before the chapel sits a man in a crimson coat. His wide-brimmed hat shadows his face. Orange-tinted glasses reflect the burning moon. Two punctured wrists rest across his knees. “You have arrived rather late,” he says. “The hospitality has suffered.” The corpse beneath him offers no answer. Yennefer studies the red coat, the ancient hands, the teeth just visible beneath a mocking smile. His body radiates a stillness no living man could maintain. “A necromancer,” she says. “Disappointing. I put so much effort into the hat.” He rises. The corpse slides from his knees and folds onto the cobblestones. “Most people call me Alucard. Some call me a monster.” His nostrils flare. “But you smell of lilac and gooseberries. Yennefer of Venneberg.” “Vengerberg. And I can call you whatever you prefer.” “Ah. The difference between power and good breeding.” The chapel door hangs open. Yennefer crosses the threshold, careful not to turn her back on him. Alucard follows. The chapel’s interior is blackened. Wooden saints crowd the walls, their faces burned away by magic that resembles no blessing. At the far end, the well waits beneath a crumbling stone arch. Its water reflects nothing. “Your objective?” he asks. “The same as yours.” “No.” He tilts his head. “Mine is older.” He draws one of his massive handguns. Yennefer does not turn. “Is that the objective?” “Yes. Although I confess my interest has improved.” Three shots split the silence. The first bullet splinters a saint above her shoulder. The second tears through the well’s stone arch. The third passes through the space where her head has been. Yennefer spins, flicking her fingers. A disc of violet light catches the bullet and throws it back. Alucard catches it between two fingers before it can strike his chest. “Interesting,” he says. The first two bullets strike him instead. Silver tears through his shoulder. His body jerks. Blood stains the red coat, then the wound closes beneath flesh that ripples like disturbed water. Yennefer’s eyes narrow. He fires again. She answers with a wave of force. The chapel’s remaining windows explode outward. The pressure catches him, lifts him from the floor, and drives him into the ceiling beam. Splinters rain around him. Alucard tears himself free and drops lightly onto the well’s rim. “Remarkable,” he says. “You make the air behave.” “Get off.” “No.” The guns roar. Yennefer throws up a shield, then flings herself sideways as its surface fractures. One bullet grazes her sleeve. Another buries itself in the floor between her boots. The third never reaches her. Alucard catches it in his mouth. He laughs around the silver. The sound is uglier than the gunfire. The chapel shudders. He straightens, adjusting the brim of his hat, and the wound in his shoulder finishes healing. Yennefer’s hand closes around the doorframe. Her knuckles pale. “Your eyes betray you,” he observes. “You intended to ask how many times I can die.” “I intended to ask whether you can stop shooting.” “Both are interesting questions.” She steps into the courtyard. He follows. They circle the chapel without closing the distance. He fires from the hip, laughing when she deflects the shots and silent when her magic catches his coat. She hurls a wall of packed snow at him; he dissolves into a flock of black birds and reforms on the chapel roof, coat settling around him as if gravity has briefly forgotten him. Yennefer cuts off the roof’s supporting beam. The building collapses between them. Alucard lands beside the well as masonry crashes into the square. His coat catches fire. He removes it, folds it, and places it carefully on a dry stone. “Most people,” he says, “would stop trying to impress me.” “I’m not trying to impress you.” “No. You’re trying to survive. It is still flattering.” The anger she suppresses transforms her features into something almost gentle. She lifts both hands. The air between them tightens. Stones rise from the courtyard, each one spinning with lethal speed. Alucard watches them rather than the witch who commands them. “You are angry,” he says. “A disappointing waste of such concentration.” The stones strike. He becomes a bat at the last instant. They pass through his shadow, shattering the chapel, the market stalls, the mounting stone where he first waited for her. When he reforms beside her, one arm hangs at an unnatural angle. The arm rights itself. Yennefer’s breathing has grown uneven. Violet light flickers around her fingers. “Again?” he asks. “Once more.” The lie lives plainly in her eyes. He notices. He does not mention it. Instead, he looks toward the empty houses. Somewhere beneath them, heartbeats hammer against cellars and cupboards. The villagers have not fled. They hide, believing their silence can preserve them. Yennefer sees where his gaze lands. “Your quarrel is not with them.” “My quarrel is wherever I choose.” “Then choose elsewhere.” He studies her beneath the blood moon. The amusement leaves his face, replaced by an older, emptier attention. “Why are you here, Yennefer?” “To obtain something I need.” “The child you cannot have?” Her magic strikes him before she can stop herself. The impact throws him across the courtyard. His back strikes the chapel wall, cracking stone around him. For once, he does not laugh. Yennefer draws a breath. “You know nothing about it.” “I know wanting,” he says, rising, “and the particular foolishness of wanting something one cannot take.” The words strike closer to bone. Alucard reaches for his coat. Beneath it rests a stake. Yennefer’s expression changes. He offers it to her. “No fight?” she asks. “I am tired of fights that end too quickly.” She examines the sharpened wood. Her fingers tremble with restrained power. The well gives a long, low groan. Black water trembles inside its circle. Neither of them looks away from the other. “Come closer, then,” she says. “Why?” “Because I may decide to accept your invitation.” He does so. The guns remain holstered. The stake remains between them. Every year of his existence weighs behind his red eyes, and for one suspended moment, the balance tilts toward ending. Yennefer could drive the stake through his heart. Alucard could let her. Neither does. Instead, he smiles—not the smile he wears for victims, but something rarer and more dangerous. Recognition. “The bird of Hermes is my name,” he says, “eating my wings to make me tame.” She lowers the stake. “No,” she says. “It is not.” Alucard offers it to her. She takes it. “Tell me your name first,” he says. “That was rude of me.” She considers. “Alucard,” she says finally. “The bird of Hermes is my name. Eating my wings to make me tame.” “Much better.” He steps back. Yennefer lets the light around her fingers fade. The chapel lies broken between them. The village lies empty. Neither has obtained what they came for. “Tell me your name first,” he says. “That was rude of me.” She considers. “Yennefer.” “Yennefer what?” “Yennefer of Vengerberg.” The guns remain holstered. The stake remains between them. Every year of his existence weighs behind his red eyes, and for one suspended moment, the balance tilts toward ending. Yennefer could drive the stake through his heart. Alucard could let her. Neither does. Instead, he smiles—not the smile he wears for victims, but something rarer and more dangerous. Recognition. “The bird of Hermes is my name,” he says, “eating my wings to make me tame.” She lowers the stake. “No,” she says. “It is not.” She turns toward the gates. Alucard retrieves his coat and shrugs it on. “Try not to die before I return.” “I make no promises.” “Wise. I dislike liars.” “And I dislike men who mistake cruelty for strength.” He laughs. This time, the sound carries something almost human. “No,” he says. “I mistake strength for the privilege of being contradicted.” At the gates, Yennefer stops beside the broken cart wheel. She rights it with one hand. The cracked rim scrapes against the mud. A black coat passes behind her, crimson bright beneath the bloody moon. She does not turn around. “Find me when you want a fight worth having,” she says. Alucard’s footsteps continue toward the empty road. “I already do.”
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical craft and atmospheric writing, successfully capturing the essence of both characters while creating a compelling encounter. The author establishes an evocative medieval setting with the blood moon imagery and abandoned village, creating an appropriately gothic atmosphere for these supernatural characters to meet. The characterization is notably strong. Alucard's sadistic playfulness, arrogance, and desire for worthy opponents comes through clearly in his dialogue and actions. His offer of the stake near the end perfectly captures his complex relationship with his own immortality. Yennefer's pride, magical prowess, and underlying vulnerability regarding her infertility are well-rendered, particularly in her visceral reaction when Alucard mentions the child she cannot have. The power dynamic shifts effectively throughout the piece, with neither character gaining clear dominance. The combat sequences are well-choreographed, showing both characters' abilities while maintaining tension. The dialogue crackles with wit and underlying menace, feeling authentic to both characters' voices. However, the piece suffers from some structural issues. There are clear repetitive passages near the end where dialogue and actions are duplicated almost verbatim, suggesting either an editing error or AI generation artifact. The pacing becomes somewhat uneven in the final third, with the resolution feeling slightly rushed after the extended combat sequence. The prose style is generally elegant, though occasionally veers toward purple prose with phrases like "Every year of his existence weighs behind his red eyes." The imagery is consistently strong, particularly the opening description of the blood moon and the destroyed village. The ending strikes an appropriate note of mutual respect and unresolved tension, avoiding both saccharine positivity and overwrought darkness. The final exchange suggests future encounters while maintaining the characters' essential natures. Prompt:
Prison Strings Jolyne Cujoh & Makima Write a story where Jolyne Cujoh (JoJo's Bizarre Adventure) and Makima (Chainsaw Man) cross paths at a supernatural prison facility. Jolyne is immediately suspicious of Makima's falsely sweet demeanor, while Makima is intrigued by Jolyne's Stand ability. Their battle of wits escalates dangerously as Jolyne realizes how manipulative Makima truly is. **Jolyne Cujoh (JoJo's Bizarre Adventure)** Jolyne is the daughter of Jotaro Kujo and the first female JoJo protagonist. Her Stand, Stone Free, allows her to unravel her body into string that she can control. She's hot-headed, foul-mouthed, and doesn't take disrespect from anyone. She was framed for murder and sent to prison. She has a distinctive butterfly tattoo on her arm and wears her hair in two buns. Despite her tough exterior, she's deeply loyal to her friends and family. She can be impulsive but is highly adaptable in battle. She inherited her father's ability to stay cool under pressure but is more emotionally expressive. Famous quote: "If there's no Mickey, this shit ain't Disney!" **Makima (Chainsaw Man)** Makima appears as a young woman with auburn hair and ringed yellow eyes. She's the Control Devil who can dominate anyone she considers beneath her (nearly everyone). She maintains a pleasant, soft-spoken demeanor that masks her manipulative, cold nature. She can create contracts with humans and devils, often exploiting their desires. She's obsessed with Chainsaw Man and wants to control him. She keeps numerous people and devils as pets on leashes. She's practically immortal due to a contract with the Prime Minister. She views humans as lesser beings but mimics human emotions perfectly. Famous quote: "It's okay. Dogs are supposed to die for their owners." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Prison Strings The chain-link fences rattle as the prisoners shuffle into the yard. Blackthorn Maximum Security has no windows, no chapel, and no sunlight. The white square marks their hour outside. Jolyne watches the other prisoners circle like fish in a drain. She keeps her shoulders loose and her eyes moving. Three weeks ago, she had been framed for murder. Now the walls measured her in days. A woman in a red coat waits on the other side of the fence. Her auburn hair is neatly tied back. Her smile is warm enough to make Jolyne suspicious of it. Two guards flank her, but neither looks at the woman. They look at their shoes. “Makima,” the woman says. “I’m here to make your stay more comfortable.” Jolyne reads the clipboard instead of the face. “Comfortable how? Better soap? A bigger cage?” Makima’s yellow eyes flick with rings like clocks frozen before noon. “Freedom. Your friends could visit. Your father’s name could be cleared, too. Wouldn’t that be nice?” Jolyne’s fingers curl. “How do you know Jotaro?” “Your file mentions him.” “My file doesn’t.” “Then I must have read somewhere else.” The answer comes too smoothly. Jolyne remembers the missing minutes after her arrest, the impossible rooms behind the interrogation doors, the guards who stopped asking questions once she stopped answering. Nobody escapes Blackthorn through kindness. Makima steps close enough for the fence to separate them. “May I?” She doesn’t wait. A soft pressure brushes Jolyne’s mind: a little girl erased from every record, alone, frightened, desperate for someone to say that the world isn’t her fault. It feels like sympathy. It feels like a hand closing around her throat. Jolyne exhales. “Try that on the next inmate.” “It’s okay,” Makima murmurs. “Dogs are supposed to die for their owners.” “Your Stand,” Makima says, pleasantly. “Stone Free. You unravel yourself into strings. I’ve heard of it.” “Yeah, and you won’t hear of it again.” Jolyne touches the fence. A strand slides from her fingertip, winds through the chain links, and jerks the entire barrier toward Makima. Makima raises one finger. The fence stops. Not because it breaks. Because every inmate in the yard stops. Their bodies remain folded beneath the weight of Makima’s will. The fence vibrates under Jolyne’s string, unable to move forward and unable to let go. Makima studies the thread with open interest. “You can reach through anything you touch.” “Only the things I choose.” “No,” Makima says. “Anything you love.” Jolyne’s strand goes slack. “It’s not control,” Jolyne says. “It’s suggestion.” “Is there a difference where you’re standing?” The fence snaps. A wave of wire crashes between them, and Makima walks through the gap as if it were a doorway. She stops just outside Jolyne’s reach. “I could let you leave. No cuffs. No trial. No sentence. You could have everything you’ve been afraid to want.” “What’s the leash made of?” Makima’s smile doesn’t falter. “Trust.” Jolyne laughs, sharp and ugly. “Yeah, that’s the collar.” “Ask for it. Ask for freedom, and I’ll give it to you. Ask for your father, and I’ll bring him here. Every wish is a door. I simply choose which ones open.” The yard vanishes. Jolyne sees sunlight through an open gate, a familiar silhouette waiting outside. For one heartbeat, she forgets the wire digging into her palms. Then she notices the shadow. It falls toward her, though the sunlight is behind the gate. It has too many hands, and every one of them ends in a leash. Jolyne yanks her string free. The vision breaks into sparks. “What the hell was that?” “A possibility,” Makima says. “Also a warning. You imagine a way out, and I decide whether it has an exit.” Jolyne’s stomach turns. She recognizes the trick now. Makima doesn’t need chains when she can make someone thank her for putting them on. “Here’s the difference between us,” Makima says. “You want your life returned. I want to hear you say it belongs to me.” “Bitch, it doesn’t.” The pressure returns. Jolyne’s knees weaken, but she locks them. Somewhere inside, a hook catches on her anger, her fear, her desperate hope that her father is safe. It isn’t obedience. It is a promise that obedience might purchase peace. Jolyne holds still until the hook stops pulling. Then she smiles. Makima’s eyes narrow. “You’re enjoying this.” “Hell, no. But you just showed your hand.” Jolyne lets the thread from her finger brush the ground. “You don’t own what people are. You own what they’re afraid to lose.” “Ah. An argument.” “It’s a diagnosis.” She pulls. Stone Free races along the concrete, through the fence, along every guard’s belt. It finds no hearts to crush, no bones to break. Instead, it loops through handcuffs, door hinges, and the underground pipes. A low groan rolls beneath the yard. The inmates gasp as one. Makima’s head turns. “What are you doing?” “Opening a door.” The fence rattles. Not from Jolyne’s string. Every inmate nearby steps aside. In the spaces between them, Jolyne glimpses figures in ragged gray, bodies transparent as old film. They pass through the concrete toward the gate, each one making the chain links shiver as they cross. Jolyne remembers the stories about Blackthorn’s basement: prisoners who vanish before their trials, then remain buried beneath the institution in unmarked cells. The dead do not fear Makima. They follow her. Jolyne pulls harder. “You buried your pets.” Makima watches the procession with a small, sincere-looking sadness. “Ownership is a promise, Jolyne. I keep every promise. Even the unpleasant ones.” The gate tears loose. Makima enters the breach, and the leash-tight pressure returns with her. Jolyne’s body unravels into string, racing through the gate’s hinges and locking around the frame. “Come with me,” Makima says. Her voice laughs through the pressure. “Make me.” She draws the lattice shut behind the Control Devil, buying one breath and one fiercely defiant hope. Strings strain against impossible weight. Beyond the wall, the fences begin to rattle again.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and character understanding within the crossover premise. The author successfully captures both Jolyne's defiant, street-smart personality and Makima's manipulative, falsely pleasant demeanor. The dialogue feels authentic to both characters, particularly Jolyne's crude directness ("Bitch, it doesn't") and Makima's deceptively gentle threats. The supernatural prison setting is well-established with economical but evocative details like "no windows, no chapel, and no sunlight" and the mysterious "impossible rooms behind the interrogation doors." The author effectively builds tension through the psychological battle between the characters, showing rather than telling how Makima's control powers work through subtle mental pressure and environmental manipulation. The prose maintains a consistent noir-ish tone that fits the prison setting while incorporating the supernatural elements naturally. Descriptions like "yellow eyes flick with rings like clocks frozen before noon" are vivid without being overwrought. The pacing builds effectively from initial suspicion to open confrontation. However, the ending feels somewhat rushed and unclear. The introduction of the ghostly prisoners and Jolyne's final gambit with her string powers lacks sufficient setup and explanation. The resolution doesn't feel fully earned, as it's unclear exactly what Jolyne has accomplished or how sustainable her resistance will be. The piece also occasionally relies on cryptic dialogue that obscures rather than illuminates the conflict. The character work is the strongest element - both protagonists feel true to their source material while being placed in a genuinely threatening situation that tests their abilities and personalities. Makima's casual cruelty and Jolyne's stubborn defiance create compelling dramatic tension throughout most of the piece. + Scp: Notes from the Future — Score: 85.2
Prompt:
Write an SCP report about a researcher who begins finding handwritten notes from their future self, warning about a containment breach that hasn't happened yet. The notes become increasingly desperate and incoherent, sometimes containing information that contradicts known reality. Include the Foundation's attempts to determine if this is an actual temporal anomaly or psychological manipulation by a contained entity, and the researcher's struggle to trust their own perception. First person (researcher's perspective with interspersed notes), past tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Item #:** SCP-████ **Object Class:** Euclid (provisional) **Addendum:** Account submitted by Dr. Elena Rusk, Site-██ I was assigned to study SCP-████, a Euclid-class entity that implanted convincing memories of conversations that had never occurred. It took a person's anxieties, repeated them until they seemed familiar, then used that familiarity to make them act against the Foundation. For six months, I had catalogued its methods without showing any sign of infection. Then I found a note bearing my signature. I assumed it was a message from my future self, written to prevent a disaster. > **14 March, 04:14** > Containment breach in thirteen days. Do not trust anyone who says we are safe. > —E.R. I was alone on the overnight shift, with the door sealed. The next note was dated 15 March. A sealed envelope had appeared under the door. The surveillance recording showed nothing, but the pressure plate registered a thirty-one-kilogram load for half a second. I weighed sixty-eight kilograms. The recording might have failed. > **15 March, 03:40** > You looked at the transcript. I am not supposed to tell you this part. > —E.R. We tested the paper and ink with microscopy, spectroscopy, X-ray fluorescence, and isotope analysis. The paper matched a watermark from a printing works demolished in 1987. The ink contained graphite, iron salts, and trace cerium and ruthenium in proportions that did not match any office pen, including my issued pen, stockroom samples, and material from SCP-████. More disturbingly, its cerium isotopes were unstable. During the second analysis, measured cerium abundance fell seventeen percent. The instruments were functioning. They were recalibrated. The result was unchanged. > **16 March** > They will say the ink is old. Ask why any old ink knows your name. > —E.R. At first, the notes resembled warnings, not prophecy. On 17 March, they identified a fault in the containment lift. I found a hairline fracture in its brake assembly. On 19 March, they described an electrical fire in the wet laboratory. I cut the circuit before smoke appeared. On 21 March, they warned me not to answer the intercom after midnight. At 04:07, SCP-████ spoke through it in my mother's voice and asked me to open its cell. I stayed silent. The intercom had no connection to containment. > **21 March, 04:07** > It heard you. > It always hears you. > —E.R. The Foundation suspected psychological manipulation before considering a temporal anomaly. I underwent personality testing, deception detection, sleep deprivation, and EEG. Other researchers forged notes in my handwriting and planted false predictions. I identified the forgeries, but became disturbed when another note correctly described a dream I had not reported. When I was sedated, the appearance of new notes stopped. When I woke, six pages of new handwriting lay on my desk, and I had no memory of writing them. > **24 March** > A sleeping mind is still a mind. They only need the paper to be quiet. > —E.R. By 27 March, the notes referred to events I could not reconcile with accepted history. One said the site director had died in 2019; records confirmed the date, but the man was alive. Another described me walking through a wing demolished before I was born. A third claimed there had never been an SCP designation and that we were both notes in a book. I underlined that sentence. The underline was mine, although I had not made it. > **28 March** > The director is dead. The east wing was never demolished. Ask the janitor. > > **29 March** > There is no site. No Foundation. No room. > Only a door. Only you. > Only me. > —E.R. The Temporal Anomalies team removed every clock from my office, replaced my pens with inert instruments, and gave me blank paper sealed in evacuated envelopes. I was told neither the date nor the questions being asked elsewhere. At 09:00, writing appeared inside an envelope watched continuously by two officers. It read, “The test is meaningless. They already know how it ends.” Security footage showed the handwriting forming stroke by stroke while I was in another building, under observation. A specialist could not distinguish it from mine. I could, but I no longer trusted my judgment to say why. > **30 March** > Thank you for the new room. I could not reach you in the old one. > —E.R. Containment breached on 27 March at 04:17. SCP-████ had been moved to a sublevel cell, but its lock showed no damage or override. A staff analyst heard her own voice outside and opened the cell manually. I was not working that night. Everyone insists I was not. My badge was in the lock, and a camera showed me entering eleven minutes earlier, although the image had no face. By 04:22, the entity was back inside. I had lost eleven minutes. It had never tried to leave. > **27 March, 04:22** > It did not try to leave. > It learned what I look like. > —E.R. The methods matched those in previous reports, favoring manipulation, but did not explain how the notes knew of the move, the test, or my dreams, or why the ink decayed. Temporal precognition could explain foreknowledge, but not the sealed envelope. We found no altered records, ink in the entity's cell, or hidden access to my office. We could not determine whether I had encountered the future or merely rehearsed it. > **2 April** > You are reading this because you succeeded. > Do not call that trust. > —E.R. I submitted this account myself because I wanted the record to contain one thing I could still choose. I no longer trusted my perception. I had recovered the missing handwriting. It was mine. It ended with a sentence I did not remember writing: “If the notes are mine, the breach is not over. If they are not, I am already part of it.” Beneath it was my signature. The paper was still warm. The ink analysis was genuine. That was supposed to comfort me. I could no longer decide whether the future was warning me, or whether some part of me had been building it.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This SCP report demonstrates a sophisticated understanding of the Foundation's clinical documentation style while crafting a genuinely unsettling psychological horror narrative. The author successfully captures the bureaucratic tone characteristic of SCP entries while maintaining the first-person researcher perspective as requested. The piece excels in its structural approach, using the interspersed notes format effectively to create mounting tension. The handwritten messages serve as both plot device and source of dread, with their content becoming increasingly fragmented and contradictory as promised. The temporal ambiguity is well-executed - the reader genuinely cannot determine whether this represents actual precognition, psychological manipulation, or something more sinister. The technical details feel authentic to the SCP universe, from the isotope analysis of the ink to the Foundation's methodical testing procedures. The author demonstrates strong world-building knowledge, referencing appropriate Foundation protocols and terminology naturally. The scientific explanations for the anomalous properties are plausible within the fictional framework. Character-wise, Dr. Rusk's deteriorating mental state is portrayed convincingly through increasingly uncertain language and self-doubt. The progression from confident researcher to someone questioning their own perception feels organic and earned. The voice remains consistent throughout, maintaining the clinical tone even as the content becomes more disturbing. The horror builds effectively through accumulating details rather than shock tactics. The revelation that the researcher may have been complicit in the breach, combined with the ambiguous ending about whether they're warning themselves or building toward disaster, creates genuine unease. However, the piece occasionally relies on telling rather than showing, particularly in explaining the Foundation's suspicions and testing procedures. Some transitions between events feel slightly abrupt, and while the clinical tone is appropriate, it sometimes distances the reader from the emotional impact. The ending is appropriately dark and ambiguous, avoiding false resolution while providing a satisfying sense of completion to the narrative arc. + Scp: Unmarked Doors Archive — Score: 79.5
Prompt:
Write an SCP entry about a series of identical unmarked doors appearing in abandoned buildings worldwide that lead to a massive, architecturally impossible archive. Documents within reference a previous global civilization destroyed by an unspecified containment failure. Foundation researchers discover references to their own organization under a different name, including personnel files for current staff dated centuries ago. Include exploration logs revealing sections of the archive actively being removed by entities resembling hazmat teams who flee when approached, and evidence that O5 Council members have visited the archive without authorization. Third person (exploration team perspective) with recovered document excerpts. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# SCP-6000 — “The Older Door” **Object Class:** Keter **Containment Status:** Contained while all confirmed entrances remain sealed ## Special Containment Procedures Confirmed entrances to SCP-6000 are sealed with mechanical locks and Class-III thaumic anchors. Each site is maintained by a civilian cover organization and monitored by two Foundation personnel. Excavation around a door requires O5 approval. Archive material must not be connected to networked storage. All documents are potentially hostile information sources, regardless of dates, seals, or authorship. Personnel must not learn that they appear in records predating their births. Recognition requires immediate amnestication and replacement. Do not open an entrance for testing. A recovered index identifying another location does not authorize a search. ## Description SCP-6000 comprises twenty-three confirmed identical doors in abandoned buildings across six continents. Each is a gray, unmarked slab with six recessed panels, no frame, and no visible hinges, handle, lock, or threshold. Despite lacking hardware, each door opens when pulled. Measurements and unknown-metal composition match across instances. The doors are older than their host buildings. A door in a 1920s railway tunnel bears 8,000–12,000 years of corrosion. Another in a seventeenth-century monastery bears patina consistent with at least 90,000 years. Oxide, sediment, and identical tool marks beneath the weathering establish that these doors predate their surroundings. Each door opens onto SCP-6000-1, an interconnected archive of unknown extent. At least nineteen subterranean levels and thousands of branching galleries have been mapped, despite the host structures enclosing less than 1,000 square metres. Interior distances exceed exterior dimensions; some corridors produce gravity toward their walls. There is no sunlight, decay, biological contamination, or identifiable light source. Recovered paper is old but does not decay at a rate consistent with its age. Foundation researchers identified the doors in 2021 after automated comparisons of pre-construction photographs with Surveyor-12 imagery. References to nineteen additional doors remain unverified. MTF Beta-7 “Maz Hatters,” assisted by Site-17 archives personnel, was dispatched to Lisbon on 2024-03-18. Linguistic consultant Dr. Maya Sorel accompanied the team. The expedition’s orders prohibit removing any document bearing a Foundation seal. ## Exploration Log 6000-03 The team opens the Lisbon door and finds a vestibule beyond it. After 400 metres, surveyors establish that the passage’s interior volume exceeds the entire Lisbon site. A flight of stairs descends 300 metres while elevation increases by two. Compasses rotate independently. The walls show no construction joints. Corridors seen through distant doorways reappear immediately behind the team. The first recovered directory is labelled “EARTH SURVIVOR INDEX / REPOSITORY CYCLE 114.” Another reads “CONTAINMENT FAILURE: MASTER REPORT.” Both use a language resembling premodern Portuguese, mixed with symbols absent from human writing. > **RECOVERED DOCUMENT 6000-1-09** > > **Containment Failure: Master Report** > > Our containment failed. The initiating condition is unavailable to this copy. > > Reconstruction is no longer possible. The homeworld’s population is lost. We cannot evacuate the people; we can preserve what they chose to keep. > > Leave the outermost repositories open. Let the survivors believe nothing survived them. A later species will need a reason to continue. > > — Directorate of Perpetual Custodianship ## Exploration Log 6000-04 Sorel identifies “Custodians” as an institutional title. A ledger dated 1608 lists “Sorel, Maya,” with a portrait matching the expedition’s consultant and the notation “active.” Other files identify the Custodians as an earlier name for the Foundation. Personnel files for three current guards carry nineteenth-century dates; Sorel’s file bears a modern photograph dated two days earlier. > **RECOVERED DOCUMENT 6000-1-31** > > **Custodians’ Continuity Mandate, 1691** > > Should this Commission fall, the successor body will be styled “the Foundation.” Its purpose will remain: keep the doors shut, and keep the record intact. > > No new mandate is required. The files include Foundation seals bearing dates after their supposed issuance. A separate index describes “twenty-three maintained thresholds.” The twenty-fourth is listed beneath the floor of the team’s Lisbon safehouse. The team withdraws while Site-17 begins structural surveys. ## Exploration Log 6000-05 At 14:22, the team hears wheeled equipment and metal cutting deeper in the archive. Six entities in sealed white suits remove shelving from “CURRENT ERA RECORDS.” Their helmets have featureless black visors; a divided-circle emblem marks their uniforms. When the team calls out, the entities abandon their carts and flee through a corridor previously found closed. They do not attack and are not pursued. The removed shelving exposes geometric voids cut into walls extending beyond survey lines. Pages along their route mention “induction review” and “continuity correction.” A crate left behind contains file covers for every expedition member. The outermost folder is labelled “OBSERVER ACCESS: THRESHOLD 24 / PENDING.” The team recovers one file and withdraws. It contains post-collapse Foundation reports and personnel assignments extending back centuries, establishing the Custodians, the Foundation, and the expedition as parts of the same continuity. ## Exploration Log 6000-07 Behind a false wall, the team finds an administrative vestibule and visitor ledger. Entries dated 1889, 1954, and 2019 identify O5-3, O5-7, and O5-11. Preserved biological samples match the current Council members’ biometrics. The “Authorization” column reads “NONE” for every visit. > **RECOVERED DOCUMENT 6000-1-88** > > **Office of Threshold Observation** > > O5-7 entered without authorization on 2019-04-02. The Council denies the visit. Delete this entry before the next recurrence. > > Retrieval personnel are not to observe the observer. ## Addendum 6000-2: Council Access Foundation records list no expedition to Lisbon by Council members. However, a 2019 Site-17 maintenance log records a door opened from inside the safehouse using O5-7’s retinal hash. No security team was dispatched, and the record was sealed before routine review. The door, ledger page, and Foundation record share a repair code absent from later databases. Council authorization can be excluded using Foundation records alone. Continued denial is therefore treated as deliberate noncompliance, not an administrative discrepancy. No Council member has acknowledged any visit. ## Addendum 6000-3: Latest File The final catalogued document bears the date 2024-03-21, three days after the Lisbon entry. It names Sorel “the successor linguist” and describes a door beneath the team’s accommodation. The file was recovered before the location was found. > **RECOVERED DOCUMENT 6000-1-112** > > **Successor Note, undated** > > When they ask what happened to the world above, show them their own files. > > They have asked before. > > — M. Sorel All confirmed entrances remain sealed. The Lisbon entrance is reinforced with a second mechanical lock. The archive has not been entered again.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This SCP entry demonstrates a sophisticated understanding of the Foundation universe's conventions while delivering a genuinely unsettling concept. The piece successfully captures the clinical, bureaucratic tone characteristic of SCP documentation, maintaining consistency throughout its technical language and procedural formatting. The central premise—doors leading to an archive containing evidence of cyclical civilizations and the Foundation's own recursive history—is both creative and philosophically disturbing. The author skillfully builds tension through the revelation that current personnel appear in centuries-old records, suggesting either time loops or something more sinister about the Foundation's nature. The exploration logs are well-structured, each revealing new layers of the mystery without overwhelming the reader. The progression from discovering the archive to finding personnel files to encountering the hazmat entities creates effective escalation. The entities fleeing when approached is a nice touch that maintains mystery while suggesting they have specific, limited objectives. The recovered documents feel authentic to the SCP format, with appropriately cryptic language that implies larger horrors without explicit exposition. The "Directorate of Perpetual Custodianship" as a predecessor organization is clever worldbuilding that fits the Foundation's secretive nature. However, the piece has some weaknesses. The character of Dr. Sorel feels somewhat underdeveloped beyond her function as a linguistic consultant, though her appearance in historical records is effectively unsettling. The exploration team members lack distinct personalities, functioning more as narrative vehicles than believable individuals. The writing occasionally becomes dense with technical details that, while appropriate for the format, can impede narrative flow. Some sections read more like actual bureaucratic reports than engaging fiction, which may be intentional but reduces emotional engagement. The ending with Sorel's note "They have asked before" is genuinely chilling and implies the horrifying possibility that this discovery is itself cyclical. The O5 Council's unauthorized visits add another layer of institutional corruption and hidden knowledge that enhances the paranoid atmosphere. The piece adheres closely to the prompt requirements, incorporating all requested elements: the doors, the archive, the previous civilization, personnel files, hazmat entities, and O5 visits. The third-person perspective and document excerpts are well-executed. + Classic sci-fi: Offworlder (Le Guin) — Score: 86.6
Prompt:
Classic sci-fi: Offworlder (Author style: Le Guin) Write a chapter following a young diplomatic envoy sent to address tensions on a distant human colony where humanity has diverged into distinct subspecies through both natural adaptation and separation of lineages. Against protocol, the envoy slips away from official functions to walk the streets alone, encountering markets, ordinary citizens, and social structures that contradict the official briefings. Upon returning to their quarters, the envoy is reprimanded by Command, and is tasked with approaching the stationed Minister of Science (a political posting rather than scientific). A challenging conversation ensues, in which the envoy's wits and will are tested, by a seasoned political operator looking to test the mettle of the offworlder. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
## The Uses of Difference By the third morning, Vey had learned to smile without appearing interested. At the official reception they stood among delegates whose names blurred together. The Republic’s briefing described a single human population: four adapted lineages, a provisional council, disputes over water, schools, and offworld quotas. It was an excellent description of a filing system. It did not yet describe a country. Vey was twenty-six and young for the post. The Minister of Science would explain the difficulties tomorrow. There were to be three more receptions that day. To reach one, Vey slipped from the ceremonial queue, pocketed the translation wafer, and covered the Republic’s insignia beneath a plain collar. This was against protocol. The street was not. The cloak had seemed sensible in transit. Here, people turned to look. Its heavy grey cloth fell to the ankles, sealed against wind and dust. Orison’s warmth lay in its clear air; many citizens wore only narrow wraps or little else. Fine silver down caught the sun along some children’s shoulders. They were not scantily dressed. Their bodies had simply been furnished for another climate. The market occupied what the maps called an unoccupied park. Stalls sold woven bread, blue-barked fruit, and water marked with household glyphs. The sellers were broad and grey, long-boned and ochre, small and yellow-eyed: adaptations taken over centuries, lineages kept apart over generations. The briefing called them subspecies. The woman selling bread called them kin. “The old send the young to argue,” she said, when Vey asked how the city governed. There were markets without speeches and houses without music. At a public pump, a clerk told two couples sharing a name that they might draw from only one household allowance. Nobody shouted. The children watched to learn where the line would move. At noon the queues separated by lineage, as neatly as if the water had inherited a family tree. A man with luminous lashes traced the omissions on Vey’s map. “Your map says one road to the university. It does not say whose children may use it, or whose certificates count when applications outnumber places. You say we are divided because your maps have made our divisions legible to you.” When Vey returned, the door displayed Command’s seal. “Your observations are unauthorized, untranslated, and inadmissible. You will report nothing until instructed.” “Is there a particular finding you disapprove of?” “The finding that you have been making findings.” The panel went dark. Then its amber light came on: **Minister of Science, first bell.** Minister Sarr arrived with a thin case and no escort. She was greying, precise, and much more patient than her file suggested. Inside lay glass tubes, seed samples, and a tablet showing thirty years of rainfall. “Hydrology,” she said. “Science. It is what the office is called.” Her gaze settled on Vey’s cloak. “You looked conspicuous.” “I looked different.” “That is what conspicuous means.” Sarr poured water into two cracked glasses. The Republic’s briefing described a technocrat who could explain crop failure and adaptation. It omitted the long tenure and patronage, and the ministry’s real work: political arithmetic in respectable clothes. “They think I am compromised,” Vey said. “So do I. But not inaccurately.” “Why warn me?” “Because you will write a report, and I do not want a flattering one.” Vey turned the glass. “What do you call accurate?” Sarr’s mouth moved, almost a smile. “A report that survives being inconvenient. The colony is governed by lineage: citizenship, marriage, migration, water. The categories are administrative.” “Also scientific,” Vey said. “A category is a tool. A tool can be used unfairly. The question is whether you see the people who bear its weight, or only the design.” “And which do you want me to see?” “The people. If you are able.” “They are not free to choose their lineages.” “Neither are you free to choose your government,” Sarr said. “Freedom is a relation, not a possession. You have learned the words. You do not yet know what they cost.” “Why tell me?” “Because you are the first offworlder sent to negotiate rather than count. This is not a quarrel between good people and bad lineages. Every good decision here enlarges some people’s freedom and other people’s obligations. Water, schooling, marriage, work. Choose a policy, and someone must pay. I need you to understand that before you choose.” “You want me to carry your evidence.” “I want you to carry the truth to people with power.” “Those are not the same.” “No. Evidence can be opened, copied, and used. Truth must be carried.” She drew from beneath the seed tray a register of names. Beside each was a fraction. “Children,” she said. “Your commission will call this injustice, or classification. The Republic is expert at the second.” “Which is it?” “That, envoy, is what I am testing.” Vey left the register untouched. “I can promise to report what I can establish. Not what your Ministry will make of it.” Sarr closed it. “And if I report it?” Vey asked. “You warned me myself.” “You will be recalled, or praised for a colony ready for administration. Neither report will be wholly false.” “You admit that?” “I am not asking for admiration. I am asking whether you have a use for a minister who will not sell you a simpler lie.” Vey drank. The water was warm, faintly metallic, and very good. “Yes,” they said. “But I will not put words in the mouths of people who cannot correct me.” Sarr looked at them for a long moment. “Keep that caution. It is more useful than courage.” Outside, rain began, though the dry season had held for a month. It struck the roof, then the market awnings, then the stone street where separate voices rose beneath one weather. Below, the lines at the pump shifted again. Vey opened a blank report. The first word was not *stability*.

[Analysis] This piece demonstrates a sophisticated understanding of Ursula K. Le Guin's literary style, successfully capturing her characteristic blend of anthropological observation, political complexity, and philosophical depth. The author has created a nuanced exploration of colonial dynamics, identity, and power structures that feels authentically Le Guinian in its approach to speculative fiction as a vehicle for examining human social organization. The adherence to instructions is excellent - the piece follows the diplomatic envoy's unauthorized exploration, the reprimand from Command, and the challenging conversation with the Minister of Science. The worldbuilding effectively presents a human colony where adaptation has created distinct lineages, and the political tensions around resource allocation and governance are well-established. The characterization is particularly strong. Vey emerges as a believable young diplomat - curious, somewhat naive, but possessing integrity and growing awareness. Minister Sarr is expertly crafted as a seasoned political operator who tests Vey's mettle through philosophical probing rather than direct confrontation. The dialogue between them crackles with intelligence and subtext, each exchange revealing character while advancing the political and philosophical themes. The prose style successfully emulates Le Guin's spare, precise language. Sentences like "Freedom is a relation, not a possession" and "Evidence can be opened, copied, and used. Truth must be carried" demonstrate the kind of aphoristic wisdom that characterizes Le Guin's work. The writing avoids purple prose while maintaining elegance and depth. The worldbuilding details are particularly effective - the adaptation markers (silver down, luminous lashes), the water allocation system organized by lineage, and the bureaucratic categories that shape daily life all feel authentic and lived-in. The emotional complexity is well-handled, avoiding simple moral judgments while exploring the genuine difficulties of governance and justice in a stratified society. + Biopunk: Polymerase Chain Reaction — Score: 79.3
Prompt:
Biopunk -- Polymerase Chain Reaction Write a chapter set in a near-future post-apocalyptic world where corporate genetic engineering was designed with built-in obsolescence—engineered DNA lasting only one generation to maximize profits before societal collapse. Follow a biohacker working with salvaged equipment to splice viable food crops for their settlement using rapidly degrading genetic material. As world building / window dressing, include details about jury-rigged lab equipment, and the physical toll (and unexpected upsides) of using untested genetic modifications as medicine. The plot of this chapter is centred around a black market contract. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# One Generation Tarin kept the blue aquarium lamp balanced on a wooden plank above the thermal cycler. The cycler had been an incubator, then a sequencing machine, and finally an assemblage of heating elements wired to a car battery. Its programming came from a kitchen slow cooker. A baking sheet, clamped over the sample chamber, served as a lid. Every component worked. None had been designed to work with another. Rain tapped through a patch in the greenhouse roof. Beyond the glass, ash filmed the settlement’s rooftops. Inside, the air smelled of hot metal, saline, and the faint sweetness of old preservatives. Sixty-three people lived in Rook now. Last winter, four had died. “That’s the last usable donor,” Tarin said. The sample occupied a finger of cloudy ice inside a cryotube. Once, it had been a proprietary wheat sequence containing salt tolerance. Now, whatever genetic material survived the coastal vault’s collapse was rapidly losing coherence. Ceregene had built decay into their licensed organisms. The sequences survived storage, seed vaults, even years of neglect. But once thawed, they came apart. “Can you copy it before it fails?” Sable asked. “I can copy fragments. Whether the fragments remain useful is a different question.” Tarin was a biohacker by trade and a geneticist by old, badly paid training. She had helped Ceregene sequence the wheat. She had also helped install the genetic brake that made its offspring sterile. The company had not patented better grain. They had patented the end of abundance. For twenty years, engineered wheat had produced enormous harvests. The following seed carried a single-generation switch. Farmers bought new grain every season, and Ceregene’s shareholders never had to worry about a competitor saving seed for free. Medicine worked the same way. Treatments replaced cells without correcting the conditions that damaged them. Repairs lasted, if the patient could afford the next course. Everything was a subscription, including survival. Now Ceregene was rubble, its shareholders dead or living behind walls. The world had inherited their crops—and forgotten how to make them fertile. Sable’s gloves were clean. Nobody in the black market could afford that luxury. “The contract pays for a blight-resistant, salt-tolerant variety suitable for planting next week,” she said. “Half now. Half when the field takes.” “And this?” Sable placed an insulated case on the workbench. Inside lay a Ceregene ampoule labelled REV-9: neural reconstruction and sensory enhancement. Designed for company executives exposed to chemical accidents. Supposed to repair damaged nerves, sharpen perception, and sustain cognition for eighteen months. The dosage had never been tested on anyone with a settlement’s worth of malnutrition. “Your payment is mostly promises,” Tarin said. “So is your crop.” Sable left with the contract and the advance payment: a sealed REV-9 ampoule, two bags of fertilizer, and enough sterile packaging to protect the trial seed. Tarin emptied a Ceregene canister onto the bench. The old label read: **Single-Generation Food Suite. Do not propagate.** The company’s ceramic-lined glass, inert seals, and UV-resistant walls were better than anything she could buy. The canisters had once stored harvested grain. Now they held saline, buffering fluid, enzymes, and fragments of a dead agricultural empire. Ceregene had designed them to preserve their products. The DNA did not need preserving nearly as long. The donor’s decay accelerated as Tarin warmed it. Every attempt to amplify the intact sequence produced a smear, the clean bands of DNA dissolving into chemical noise. Each failed run consumed what little usable material remained. Rook’s own wheat was coarse, low-yielding, and resistant to grey blight. It was also painfully sensitive to salt. Tarin’s plan was to splice the surviving donor fragment into the old stock and hope the cross diluted Ceregene’s generation-ending brake. Hope was not a control group. She mixed REV-9 with saline in one of the empty canisters. The drug entered her as a cold shock, then heat. For two days she barely left the cot. Fever made the walls shimmer. Her muscles cramped, her stomach emptied itself repeatedly, and her left hand developed a numbness that faded only when she moved it. The new nerve pathways seemed to inflame the old injuries around them. REV-9 did not simply repair tissue; it forced her body to accept unfamiliar versions of itself. She lost seven pounds. Appetite vanished. Sleep became a bruised, intermittent thing. On the third morning, Tarin returned to the bench because the pain was less distracting than stillness. That was when she noticed the difference. The aquarium lamp looked brighter. The slow cooker’s display was legible from across the room. More remarkably, the thermal cycler’s vibration had acquired a visible texture: a wavering line running through the baking-sheet clamp, bending where the motor strained. The developing gel showed a faint stain before it resolved into distinct bands. She could sense the difference between a broken sequence and a damaged instrument by looking at them. REV-9 had sharpened her perception beyond anything Ceregene’s clinical notes admitted. It was a useful thing, purchased with pain. On the sixth day, one seed finally germinated. Seven days later, a second emerged. Its roots were pale, thin, and stubborn. The old wheat’s blight resistance seemed to have survived the splice. The donor’s salt tolerance was less certain. Germination was not proof. It did not demonstrate a field-worthy yield, a complete genome, or a second fertile generation. But the seed had not died. Tarin completed the contract and delivered the remaining grain to Sable’s agents. The payment bought fertilizer, replacement gloves, and a week without needing to eat the trial stock. The drug was not. “We need to test the rest,” Sable said at the greenhouse door. “And we cannot supervise another season. My people are hungry, but they are not patient.” “For the wheat or the drug?” Sable’s expression did not change. “Everything.” After the buyer left, Tarin carried the two surviving seedlings into the settlement’s greenhouse. She would grow them for seed, though no one could yet promise what they would become. The fertilizer would stretch across the remaining trial plots. Her hands would shake for weeks. REV-9 kept rebuilding nerves in ways her immune system still rejected. The price had not vanished. It was simply deferred. That night, Tarin found the empty REV-9 canister and turned it toward the blue light. The corporate lettering had nearly worn away. **ONE GENERATION.** She drew a line through it. Outside, rain washed ash from the greenhouse roof. Inside, two green blades leaned toward a lamp made for fish. They were not a revolution. They were a beginning.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This biopunk piece demonstrates strong technical execution and worldbuilding within the specified parameters. The author successfully creates a post-apocalyptic setting where corporate genetic engineering with built-in obsolescence has collapsed civilization, leaving survivors to work with degrading genetic material using jury-rigged equipment. The worldbuilding is particularly effective, with vivid details of improvised laboratory equipment - the thermal cycler cobbled together from various components, the aquarium lamp serving as lighting, and repurposed Ceregene canisters. The concept of engineered obsolescence in both crops and medicine creates a believable dystopian framework that feels both scientifically plausible and thematically resonant. Tarin emerges as a well-developed protagonist with clear motivation and expertise. Her background as both a former Ceregene employee and current settlement biohacker creates compelling internal conflict. The physical toll of using REV-9 is convincingly portrayed through specific symptoms and recovery details, while the unexpected enhancement of her perception provides a meaningful trade-off rather than simple benefit. The prose maintains a consistent, measured tone throughout, avoiding both overwrought drama and clinical detachment. Technical details are integrated naturally without becoming exposition dumps. The pacing moves steadily from setup through experimentation to resolution without unnecessary diversions. The black market contract provides adequate plot structure, though it functions more as a framework for exploring the world and character than as a driving dramatic force. Sable serves her purpose as a business contact but remains somewhat underdeveloped. The ending strikes an appropriate balance - neither falsely optimistic nor gratuitously dark. The two surviving seedlings represent genuine progress earned through Tarin's expertise and sacrifice, while acknowledging the ongoing challenges ahead. The symbolic crossing out of "ONE GENERATION" provides satisfying closure without overstating the achievement. Some elements could be stronger. The dialogue, while functional, lacks distinctive voice or memorable exchanges. Certain plot elements, like the specific terms of the black market deal, could use more development. The piece occasionally tells rather than shows, particularly in explaining the corporate backstory. Overall, this is competent speculative fiction that fulfills its brief effectively, with strong worldbuilding, believable science, and a protagonist whose actions feel earned and meaningful within the established context.
