+ Humour: Sisyphus Gives Advice — Score: 82.5
Prompt:
Sisyphus Gives Advice Write a comedic scene in the style of Terry Pratchett featuring Sisyphus, who has started an advice column while continuing his eternal boulder-pushing. Rather than being bitter about his punishment, Sisyphus has developed a comfortably zen emotional intelligence and wisdom from his centuries of repetitive labor. Not in the cliche ways you might expect -- he's actually very grounded, warm & connected with the everyday human plight. He dictates responses to "Crow," his feathered familiar who serves as both scribe and mail carrier. The piece should include Sisyphus thoughtfully answering several advice-seekers' letters about everyday problems (relationship troubles, work-life balance, dealing with difficult people, life purpose doubts) while periodically returning to his boulder-pushing duties. His advice should be surprisingly insightful and practical. The humor should emerge naturally from the messages he receives, from mundane to risque. Sisyphus should genuinely enjoy helping others, finding meaning in this new pursuit while maintaining his boulder routine. The humour should be *understated and not forced*. Contrary to expectation, almost none of his advice involves boulder rolling metaphors (though he does sneak *one* subtle in there), nor a treatise on stoicism. We are also going against the obvious fish-out-of-water trope; in fact, he's surprisingly a natural at this. In all of this , it's important to *show, don't tell*. The format should be largely epistolary, with the occasional interjection for scene setting. 1000 words.
Model Output:
## Sisyphus Gives Advice Crow was perched on a flat stone with a letter bag tied to her ankle, a writing leaf on her knee, and an expression of professional dignity. The leaf was Sisyphus’s contribution. The rest had been Crow’s idea. “The biscuit isn’t a bribe,” she said, having examined the small envelope with some care. “The sender seems to think it’s a bribe.” “Then it’s a biscuit with poor boundaries,” said Sisyphus. He offered her the ink, settled himself beside the boulder, and dictated the afternoon’s correspondence. The boulder was not going anywhere. Neither was Crow, unless the biscuits ran out. “First one, please.” “The one about love and biscuits.” “There aren’t biscuits in it.” “Read it properly. I was breathing.” Crow cleared her throat with the resonant authority of somebody who could make a career of clearing throats. > **Dear Mr Sisyphus,** > > My husband is not unkind. He is simply a man who believes marriage is mostly administration. > > I told him I felt lonely. He asked whether the lawnmower had enough petrol. I have begun talking to the lawnmower. It is a poor conversationalist, but at least it doesn’t interrupt. > > I am told your letters should be accompanied by a biscuit. I have enclosed one. Please do not mistake this for a bribe. > > Molly “Molly,” Sisyphus began, “don’t try to settle a whole marriage over one biscuit. That’s rather a lot of responsibility for a shortbread.” Crow’s beak moved towards a smile. “The lawnmower is a safe subject, but it can’t do all the work. Tell your husband what you miss, and give him a sentence he can actually act on. ‘I miss you’ is good. ‘You never ask how I am’ gives him nowhere to begin. ‘I’d like an evening when neither of us is doing jobs’ is better. You can also do something you like. Take a walk. Read in the bath. Find out what the lawnmower thinks about romance.” “And if he won’t try even that?” asked Crow. “Then Molly will know where she stands, which is more than the biscuit could tell her.” > **Dear Mr Sisyphus,** > > I finish work at six and have two children too young to make toast but old enough to say “why?”. I do the shopping, the cooking, the washing, and a convincing impression of patience. > > On Sundays I lie on the floor until somebody needs me. > > My wife says I need a hobby. I looked into birdwatching, but I gather the hours are difficult. How do I get my evenings back? > > Daniel Sisyphus considered this while a beetle completed an unhurried journey across his boot. “Don’t wait until the children are asleep,” he said. “By then, the day has been given away.” He dictated a little more slowly. “Take forty minutes before they go to bed and agree that it is not for chores. Both of you get forty minutes. Make a cup of tea. Read three pages. Sit in the garden if the weather allows. Protect that time, or it will vanish along with the clean laundry. You can explain that you both come home with very little left, rather than trying to be cheerful at somebody who has been talking at you for six hours. That conversation works better than pretending to enjoy a programme you can’t hear over the kettle.” Crow wrote: *Both of you get forty minutes.* Then underlined *both*. “A hobby doesn’t have to become a passion,” Sisyphus added. “It can simply be a place to put your hands and your attention for a little while.” > **Dear Mr Sisyphus,** > > My manager is a kind man who treats every piece of my work as a minor personal disappointment. He corrects spreadsheets without changing a single figure. He says, “Don’t worry, I’ll handle it,” and then takes over the entire project. He signs off my work as “Reviewed”. > > I have started imagining him eating my lunch. Does this make me unreasonable? > > Melanie “No,” said Sisyphus. “It makes you tired, which is different.” Crow’s writing leaf came to a standstill. “Don’t try to improve his character,” he continued. “Improve the arrangements. Keep copies of your work. Ask him to record his decisions in writing. When he reaches for your keyboard, say, ‘What would you like changed?’ A question about the spreadsheet is harder for him to turn into a conversation about your character.” Sisyphus took a sip of water. “And if he still needs the last word, Melanie should look for other work. She isn’t obliged to keep supplying him with a platform. Meanwhile, she should eat her lunch somewhere else. It has done nothing wrong.” “I like that,” said Crow. “You have an alarming weakness for good advice.” “It’s very neatly arranged.” > **Dear Mr Sisyphus,** > > I am thirty-two. I have a job I can tolerate, a kind partner, and no obvious talent. Everyone I meet seems to have a calling. Mine appears to be delaying the search for one. > > Have I missed something? > > Clive Sisyphus looked over the letters. Beyond them, the road wound down through a country doing its best without the benefit of a destiny. “Clive, I don’t think a life is a parcel waiting to be delivered,” he said. “The word ‘purpose’ has done quite enough damage already. Give something away. Learn something. Mend something. Help at the library, grow beans, take a course. Try it for a month and see how you feel when it’s finished.” Crow waited. “If you like it, carry on. If you don’t, try something else. No trumpet required. He doesn’t need to become useful to millions before he’s permitted to like his Tuesday.” That was the last letter. Sisyphus dictated the replies, corrected one comma, and approved of a final sentence only after Crow had promised not to improve it. At that moment, a minor deity arrived to inspect the hill. His province was lost buttons, though he had brought a spare in case a useful criticism fell off his robe. “You could be doing so much more,” he said. “You could put a curse on the lawnmower. Shift the bus timetable. Give the manager a week of headaches. Tell Clive his purpose is to become a better man. There’d be time left over for hobbies.” “There is,” Sisyphus agreed. “Instead, you are dealing with biscuits.” “Mostly.” The deity looked at the letters as though one had bitten him. “You are wasting your divinity.” “Possibly,” said Sisyphus. “But if I solved it for them, they’d have the same trouble next Thursday and no idea what to do with it. That isn’t helping. That’s a clerical error.” The deity opened his mouth, perhaps to issue a small miracle of his own. Sisyphus had already turned his attention to the boulder. Crow packed the replies into her mailbag. Sisyphus placed his shoulder against the stone and began the long walk down. “Any last thoughts?” asked Crow. “Not until we reach the bottom,” he said. “I find I think better when I’m not going uphill.”
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates a sophisticated understanding of both the prompt requirements and Terry Pratchett's distinctive style. The author successfully creates an understated comedic voice that feels authentically Pratchettesque without falling into pastiche. The characterization of Sisyphus is particularly well-executed - he comes across as genuinely wise and grounded rather than bitter, with his advice feeling earned through experience rather than philosophical posturing. The epistolary format works effectively, with each letter presenting distinct voices and realistic problems. The advice given is practical and insightful, avoiding the obvious boulder metaphors the prompt specifically warned against (though one subtle reference is skillfully woven in with "I find I think better when I'm not going uphill"). The relationship between Sisyphus and Crow feels natural and lived-in, with their banter providing gentle humor without forced comedy. The prose style captures Pratchett's economy of language and dry wit. Phrases like "a biscuit with poor boundaries" and "It has done nothing wrong" (about the lunch) demonstrate the author's grasp of Pratchett's ability to find humor in unexpected places through precise word choice rather than elaborate setups. The piece shows rather than tells throughout - we understand Sisyphus's character through his responses and interactions rather than exposition. The minor deity's appearance at the end provides effective contrast and reinforces the themes without being heavy-handed. The ending feels natural and avoids false uplift while maintaining the established tone. However, the piece occasionally feels slightly mechanical in its structure, moving through the letters in a somewhat predictable pattern. While the advice is good, some responses could have been more distinctive to Sisyphus specifically. The imagery, while competent, doesn't quite reach the vivid, memorable quality of Pratchett's best work. + Coming of age: Lost & Found in Osaka — Score: 72.0
Prompt:
Lost & Found in Osaka Slice of Life / Coming-of-Age: First Connection. Write one scene within a larger story set in Osaka, Japan. A shy, introverted teenager & synthesizer nerd, is browsing the electronics district of Den Den Town. She is drawn to the sound of an electric guitar. A girl, slightly older and radiating confidence, is busking near the entrance to a crowded arcade, playing a blistering rendition of a classic anime theme. The scene takes us through their initial awkward interaction, transitioning into a surprisingly easy conversation. The busker, intrigued by the teenager's quiet intensity and knowledge of music, suggests they grab some sushi at a nearby kaitenzushi (conveyor belt sushi) restaurant. Write primarily in dialogue, capturing the distinct voices of the two characters: the teenager's hesitant and -- initially -- awkward speech, and the busker's more outgoing and playful tone. 1000 words.
Model Output:
## Lost & Found in Osaka At 6:43 p.m., the electronics shops of Den Den Town were beginning to switch off their signs one by one. Behind Mio, a secondhand music-equipment store displayed a row of aging synthesizer modules beneath a handwritten notice: **ALL AS IS. NO MAGIC INCLUDED.** She had come for a MIDI cable. She had left without it. The guitar reached her first. Not just volume—though the arcade entrance made even an ordinary chord feel larger than life—but the space between the notes. A bright, climbing riff cut through the traffic, the pachinko machines, the canned demonstrations from a nearby shop. Her fingers copied half a phrase against the strap of her bag. Mio stopped. One headphone hung loose around her neck. Her thumb worried the frayed edge of its cable. “Good grief!” called a girl beside the arcade, stopping the riff with a ringing final note. “I was starting to think I had to compete with a forklift.” She stood with an electric guitar slung low against her hip, one boot tapping time that had already ended. Her dark hair was tied in a messy knot, and there was a fresh scrape of dust on her sleeve. “Sorry,” Mio said. “I wasn’t—I wasn’t trying to listen.” “You were doing an excellent job of failing not to.” “I—sorry.” The girl’s stern expression broke into a grin. “Kid, you’re going to use up a week’s apologies before dessert.” Mio took half a step backward. “You played ‘Tank!’” she said quickly. Something sharpened in the girl’s attention. “Did you?” “The opening. From *Cowboy Bebop*. The theme usually goes to the brass, but you—your guitar was doing the bass line’s rhythm.” Mio swallowed. “It worked.” “Of course it worked. I’ve been practicing for eleven years.” “I meant—yes. It worked.” A group of arcade customers wandered past, coins jingling in their pockets. The girl plugged a cable into a small amplifier and offered Mio a bow exaggerated enough for a concert hall. “Aya,” she said. “Nineteen, occasionally sensible. And you are?” “Mio.” “Seventeen?” Mio nodded. “Excellent. Seventeen is old enough to appreciate a mediocre guitar solo.” “I didn’t say it was mediocre.” “I know. That’s why I’m smiling.” Aya tilted her head. “What did you think of the second solo?” “The second one?” “Mm-hm. The one where I probably invented a note that isn’t in the song.” Mio looked down at the guitar. “There was a B-flat in the turnaround.” “There was?” “You mouthed it.” “I did not.” “You did. Just now. When you said ‘there was.’” Aya stared at her. Then she laughed, sudden and delighted. “Okay. You can stop apologizing for having ears.” Mio’s mouth twitched—not quite a smile, but its cautious preliminary. “There’s a kaitenzushi place near the canal,” Aya continued. “Tiny plates, questionable lighting, excellent conveyor-belt suspense. Come with me. You can tell me whether I’m emotionally misrepresenting a bass solo.” “I don’t—people don’t usually—” “Stay if you want. Or don’t. No pressure.” Aya picked up her guitar case. “But I’ve been trying to explain the bass line in ‘The Real Folk Blues’ to people for three years, and you’ve already caught more mistakes than anyone under thirty.” Mio glanced toward the electronics street. “My sister needs me to come home for dinner.” “Then the canal’s too far. Another time?” It was so easily offered that Mio found herself nodding before she could calculate the appropriate response. “Okay.” “Wonderful. Try not to look overwhelmed.” “I’m not—people don’t usually…” “Invite you to sushi after calling your playing mediocre?” “No, they don’t.” “Wrong,” Aya said. “I do that all the time.” They fell into step beside the canal. The evening crowd moved toward the brighter lights, but Aya walked with the unhurried confidence of someone who knew the short cuts and expected company to keep pace. “So,” she said. “Mio. Synthesizer nerd?” “...Yes.” “Guitar, then?” “I like listening to it.” “From your face, you like taking it apart in your head.” “I noticed the delay,” Mio said. “It wasn’t the usual single-tap kind. The repeats overlapped. The solo had more edges, but the space around it stayed... clear.” Aya slowed. “Huh.” “Sorry.” “No, don’t apologize. Keep going.” “I’m trying.” “I noticed that too.” At the restaurant, they chose seats beside the conveyor. A weathered sign promised **120 YEN PER PLATE**, underlined twice. Aya pushed a plate of tamago toward Mio. “Right. Important question. Are you a wasabi person?” “No.” “Coward.” “Wasabi is hot.” “Hot is a state of mind.” “That doesn’t make it less hot.” Aya laughed. “Fair ruling.” Mio ate slowly, listening to Aya describe the day’s street performance: an impatient salaryman, a child who knew every word to “The Real Folk Blues,” and a tourist who had applauded during the wrong song. “I knew the tune,” Mio said. “I mean—everyone who watches *Cowboy Bebop* knows it.” “Not everyone. Most people know the opening, then forget the rest.” “‘Blue’ is better.” Aya set down her chopsticks. “I was hoping you’d say that.” “Why?” “Because ‘Blue’ has a bass line that sounds simple until you listen to what it’s doing underneath. And when the melody comes in, it doesn’t overpower it. It—” Aya waved her chopsticks vaguely. “It makes room for the sadness.” Mio nodded, more vigorously than intended. “Exactly. It’s the same bass line from ‘The Real Folk Blues,’ but it’s denser. Like someone trying to say one thing while thinking ten others.” Aya stared at her. “That was beautifully precise.” “It’s just oscillators.” “Oscillators can be poetic.” Mio lowered her eyes, smiling into her rice. A green plate carrying cucumber salad arrived between them. Aya turned it, inspecting the price sticker. “Kaitenzushi suspense,” she announced. “The suspense is terrible.” Mio glanced at the sticker. “They’ve mislabeled it again.” “Terror.” “It says 120 yen.” “Terror,” Aya agreed, taking the plate. They ate. Aya asked about Mio’s synthesizer, careful not to turn the questions into an interrogation. Mio answered in fragments at first, then discovered that talking about filters and chord progressions did not require eye contact. “It’s easier to explain music than conversation,” she admitted. “Only because music has already agreed with you halfway.” “That isn’t how music works.” “It is today. I vote.” Mio laughed. It came out startled, and she immediately looked surprised by it. Aya raised her water glass. “To music agreeing halfway.” They clinked glasses. “Do you have a favorite Kanno piece?” Mio asked. “‘Adieu.’” Mio looked up. “The live version?” “You know it?” “‘The one that starts as if it’s a quiet conversation and ends like an empty room.’” Aya’s playful expression softened. “That’s exactly what it sounds like.” “The recorded version is warmer. More people. But the live version is—” “Someone leaving.” Mio nodded. Aya was quiet for once, but not the uncomfortable kind. Her finger traced the rim of her glass. “The first time I played it,” she said, “I stopped halfway through. People didn’t notice. I just… couldn’t keep pretending the song wasn’t about anything.” “I understand.” “Do you?” “Not completely. But I recognize the impulse. You can know something perfectly and still not know what to do with it.” Aya looked at her. “Yes. Exactly that.” The belt clanked softly behind them. Neither girl reached for another plate. “I make playlists,” Aya said. “If you ever want to trade. Very niche. Possibly illegal levels of enthusiasm.” “What kind?” “‘Ghost in the Shell.’ ‘Turn A Gundam.’ Soundtracks I know nobody else owns. And whatever bizarre electronic rabbit hole you send me down.” Mio’s hands tightened around her water glass. “I—yes. I’d like that.” “Good.” Aya took out her phone. “Can I add you? For musical consultations. And proof that Den Den Town contains more than arcades.” Mio nodded, already fumbling for her own phone. “Aya?” “Mm-hm?” “Your solo wasn’t mediocre.” Aya’s smile returned, warm and ridiculously pleased. “First,” she said, “you’re still the second person to say that.” “Second?” “My guitar teacher said the same thing.” Mio looked down at the phone, smiling. The evening noise of Osaka continued around them, endless and bright, but at their table there was room for silence, and neither of them seemed afraid of it.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical craft and adherence to the prompt requirements. The author successfully creates two distinct character voices through dialogue - Mio's hesitant, fragmented speech patterns effectively contrast with Aya's confident, playful tone. The setting of Den Den Town is authentically rendered with specific details like the "ALL AS IS. NO MAGIC INCLUDED" sign and the kaitenzushi restaurant. The dialogue carries the narrative effectively, revealing character through speech patterns and musical knowledge rather than exposition. Mio's social anxiety is conveyed through her repetitive apologies and incomplete sentences, while Aya's warmth emerges through her teasing yet encouraging responses. The musical discussions feel authentic and serve as a natural bridge between the characters. However, the piece suffers from some structural issues. The opening section, while atmospheric, takes considerable time before the characters meet, reducing space for their interaction. The transition from street encounter to restaurant feels somewhat rushed, and the connection between the characters, while sweet, develops quite rapidly for someone as socially anxious as Mio is portrayed to be. The prose occasionally veers toward the precious, with phrases like "oscillators can be poetic" and overly detailed descriptions of musical nuances that feel more writerly than natural. Some dialogue exchanges, particularly around the musical analysis, read as slightly artificial - too perfectly articulated for casual conversation between teenagers. The emotional arc is gentle and believable within the slice-of-life genre, though the ending perhaps resolves a bit too neatly. Mio's transformation from extreme shyness to comfortable conversation happens within a single scene, which strains credibility slightly. The piece succeeds in creating a warm, hopeful tone without forcing dramatic change, but the character growth feels somewhat accelerated. The writing demonstrates good technical control with varied sentence structures and effective use of specific details. The cultural setting feels researched and authentic rather than superficial. The focus on music as a connecting force between the characters is well-executed and provides meaningful common ground for their interaction. + Teen horror: Tick Tock (Goosebumps) — Score: 73.0
Prompt:
Teen Horror (Goosebumps style) Write a chapter where a middle school student discovers their new smart watch has the ability to rewind time, but doesn't realize that each use is aging them until they notice physical changes (like accelerating through puberty) and that people are treating them differently. They inadvertently cause a timeline shift with disastrous consequences -- and it can only be rectified (maybe?) by reversing the clock once more. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
## The Last Second Ellie was twelve years old, which was old enough to know better than to open a mysterious present and young enough to do it anyway. The box contained a silver smartwatch with a black screen. No brand. No model number. Not even a stupid Wi-Fi password sticker. “Probably a knockoff,” Dad said. “But it works.” He was already heading toward the kitchen when Ellie fastened it around her wrist. The display lit up. **7:43 A.M.** Beneath the time was a single button. **REWIND** She tapped it. The second hand jumped backward. Her father’s chair scraped toward the table. The refrigerator door swung shut. A spoonful of oatmeal arced neatly back into its bowl. Ellie blinked. Her father blinked. “You have to turn it off,” he called after her. She couldn’t. She tried pressing the button again, but nothing happened. The watch was warm against her skin. For a moment, she could have sworn she heard a tiny voice counting backward. Then the screen returned to normal. Ellie forgot about it. That happened sometimes with presents. On the first day of seventh grade, a stack of books crashed into her knees in the hallway. A group of eighth-graders laughed. “Watch where you’re going,” one of them said. Ellie’s palms hit the floor before she realized she was falling. She pressed REWIND. The books flew upward. The boy’s laughter reversed into a cough. Ellie staggered back, catching herself upright half a second before the books landed. This time, the second hand spun smoothly backward. The books dropped into her arms. The boy stared at her. “You just—” The bell rang. Ellie hurried away, polishing the watch with her sleeve. It felt feverish. Probably because she’d run. That was all. At first, rewinding four seconds barely seemed worth mentioning. But soon Ellie was using it constantly. She rewound when a joke was made at her expense. When someone spilled soda on her backpack. When she forgot an answer during a presentation. Once, she even rewound a math test she’d failed. The watch pulsed blue. The teacher began speaking again. This time, Ellie’s paper was covered in correct answers. Her own handwriting. She didn’t remember writing them. The strange thing was that nobody questioned how she knew so much. Older students asked her opinion about parties she didn’t remember attending. Teachers spoke to her as if she were years ahead of the rest of the class. At lunch, a boy she barely knew said, “See you later, Ellie.” She had never met him before. “What do you mean?” she asked. He stared at her like she’d said something sick. “We have a thing,” he whispered. “At the arcade. Don’t forget again.” Ellie had no idea what he meant. By October, her jeans were held together with a belt. Her voice had cracked, deepened, then cracked again. Hair brushed her shoulders. Her face was losing its roundness, sharpening into someone older and much more tired. She needed a new bra. That was when she noticed the countdown. Late one night, she glanced at the watch and froze. **04:17:32** The time was 10:48. The numbers were still moving. **04:17:31** **04:17:30** Ellie tapped the face. REWIND disappeared. The countdown didn’t. She shook the watch. Removed the battery. Pried open the back. Nothing worked. When she looked up, her little brother was standing in the doorway. “You look old,” he said. “Thanks.” “Mom says we’re going to Gran’s for Thanksgiving.” Ellie nodded. Something was wrong with that. She was certain her parents hadn’t mentioned Thanksgiving. But when she went to ask them, they acted as if she was being ridiculous. “We’ve made those plans for months,” Mom said. Ellie went upstairs. She was fifteen, maybe. Or sixteen. She felt ancient. Her knees ached when she climbed the stairs. At school, the younger kids called her Miss Walker. Her old friends had disappeared—not cruelly, but completely. They no longer shared her classes, her table, or her memories. Ellie began to understand. The watch wasn’t rewinding the world. It was rewriting it. And somehow, every stolen moment came from her. The countdown fell faster. **00:59:59** **00:59:58** Sometimes it flickered at the bottom of the watch face. **ONE REPLAY REMAINING** Ellie stopped using the rewind button. The world didn’t stop changing. A storm arrived before the calendar said December. The first drops struck the middle school windows as lightning forked across the sky. Ellie was in the hallway when the lights went out. A crash echoed from the gym. Then another. Students screamed. Emergency alarms shrieked—even though no one had touched them. Ellie pressed her palm against the wall. The whole building shuddered. Through the window, she saw a car lift off the street. The storm outside was barely a drizzle. But rain was pouring from a ruptured water main, flooding the parking lot. The old gym roof, supposedly replaced twelve years ago, crumbled like wet cardboard. Ellie understood with sick clarity. She hadn’t stopped time. She had pulled the future into the present. The countdown on her watch reached zero. For one suspended second, everything was silent. Ellie looked at the REWIND button. Then at the gym, where someone was hammering against the locked doors. She pressed the button. The world screamed backward. Sirens unwound. Floodwater reversed into pipes. Pieces of ceiling flew upward, reassembling themselves. Car doors slammed shut on empty seats. The cry of a trapped child shortened into silence. Ellie’s watch burned into her skin. She tried to let go. It wouldn’t let her. She felt her hand age beneath her fingers. Tendons tightened. Skin thinned. Joints swollen. Her teeth loosened, and something crawled along her spine as if her bones were turning to stone. She was ancient. She was still twelve. The countdown restarted. **00:59:59** Ellie held on until the gym roof was whole again. Until the alarms stopped. Until the water main stopped screaming. Until the world was safe. Then she closed her eyes. When she opened them, she was lying on her bedroom floor. Morning sunlight crossed the carpet. “M Ellie!” Mom called from downstairs. “You’re going to be late!” Ellie sat up. Her hands were small. Her jeans fit. She was twelve again. She stumbled to her desk. The smartwatch sat inside its open box, dark and cold. In her pocket, she found a folded piece of paper. It was written in her handwriting. **DON’T LET IT TAKE ANYTHING ELSE.** Ellie’s mother called again. Ellie looked at the watch. The screen suddenly flickered to life. **23:59:59** **23:59:58** For one hopeful moment, the countdown held. Then REWIND began to glow again.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong adherence to the Goosebumps-style teen horror prompt, successfully incorporating all required elements: a middle schooler discovering a time-rewinding smartwatch, physical aging consequences, timeline disruption, and the need for one final rewind to fix things. The author captures the appropriate tone for the genre - accessible yet unsettling, with age-appropriate scares. The narrative structure is well-constructed, building tension through escalating use of the watch and increasingly severe consequences. The concept of the watch rewriting reality rather than simply rewinding time is clever and adds complexity beyond typical time-travel stories. The physical aging serves as an effective horror element, particularly the detail about needing a new bra and her brother's blunt observation that "you look old." Character actions remain believable throughout - Ellie's initial experimentation with the watch, her escalating reliance on it for minor inconveniences, and her horror upon discovering the countdown all feel authentic to a twelve-year-old's psychology. The supporting characters, while minimal, serve their purposes effectively. The prose maintains consistent quality with some genuinely striking moments: "She was ancient. She was still twelve" effectively captures the horror of her situation. The imagery of the world "screaming backward" during the final rewind is visceral and memorable. The pacing builds effectively from mundane school problems to catastrophic timeline collapse. However, the piece has notable weaknesses. The dialogue, while functional, lacks distinctiveness - characters speak in generic voices without individual personality markers. The ending, while appropriately dark for the genre, feels somewhat rushed in its resolution. The note from her future self ("DON'T LET IT TAKE ANYTHING ELSE") serves as convenient exposition rather than organic storytelling. Some plot elements strain credibility - particularly how quickly and completely other characters accept Ellie's apparent aging and changed circumstances. The mechanism by which the watch causes environmental disasters (gym roof collapse, flooding) feels disconnected from the established time-manipulation rules. The emotional core works well, capturing Ellie's growing isolation and horror as she realizes the true cost of her power. The final image of the countdown restarting provides an appropriately ominous conclusion that fits the genre's conventions. Prompt:
Carnival of Dangerous Intentions Coney Island, New York, July 1937. She stopped just before reaching the shooting gallery set up along the boardwalk. It was near dusk, and the carnival lights were buzzing on. **His locks**. The words flashed through her mind, again, like an intruder. Such an old-fashioned turn of phrase that kept surfacing, and something else -- dangerously compelling -- quickly suppressed, lest she question why she had returned here at all. This place where she had promised to meet the stranger -- the young man with the obsidian curls and even darker eyes. She didn't even know his name. Write a scene in a larger story inspired by this prompt. The scene should capture an atmosphere that blends romantic allure with an undercurrent of subtle danger or moral ambiguity. Think 50 shades, but with a more restrained classic sensibility. The scene is all about establishing tension. Write for the feminine perspective. Include roughly 50% dialogue, 20% internal monologue, and 30% exposition and scene setting. The tone should have some edge to it. 1000 words.

## Carnival of Dangerous Intentions Clara stopped beneath the shooting gallery’s tin stars. Beyond it, Coney Island hung its paper moons above the darkening sea. The crowd pressed past, thick with cigar smoke and hot grease. A carousel organ played three notes, stopped, and began again. She felt the rhythm under her ribs. *His locks.* The phrase had appeared in his letter among instructions: *Come at dusk. Look for the man with dark hair. You will know him by his eyes.* She had not known him then. She did not know him now. Yet here she was, carrying the strangeness beneath her silk like a stone in a shoe. A young man rose across the gallery’s mouth. The word *young* deceived. There was nothing boyish in his black, steady gaze. He removed his hat. A curl fell over his brow, black as the water beneath the pier. “You came,” he said. “You wrote.” “I did.” “Your letter was optimistic.” “Was it?” “And if I don’t know you?” His eyes considered her, unhurried. “Then I shall have to earn the acquaintance.” “And if I remember you?” His smile changed. “You won’t.” “How discourteous.” “Accurate.” A practiced reply, delivered with warmth that made caution seem unfashionable. She distrusted the feeling more than the line. “Your gloves are impractical.” “It’s July.” “That isn’t an argument for surrender.” He lifted her hand. His kiss grazed the linen, brief, courteous, wrong. Heat lingered at her knuckles. “Do I know you?” “I think you do.” “You shouldn’t say such things to a woman who can’t remember her own.” “Which woman, precisely?” “The one standing here.” “Scarcely the woman I remember.” A vendor turned the corner, his drum painted the deep blue of evening. Pink sugar wound around a stick, white as a moon that had never known dirt. The smell caught in Clara’s throat. *A child’s sticky hand. A woman bending close, her face hidden by a yellow hat. A music box giving three notes, then silence. The stranger’s younger face, and her own voice saying, Again.* The image dissolved before she could hold it. “My mother brought me here,” she said. “Twice a year. Always in June.” “She died last winter.” “I’m sorry.” Not one of his words had been cruel. She had begun, without noticing, to listen for cruelty and find only kindness. That was less comforting. “You remember her.” “She wore yellow when she meant for you to remember her.” Clara’s hand tightened inside its glove. “What do you mean?” “I mean you have forgotten something you wished you hadn’t.” “Do you know what happened to me?” “No.” It was the first answer she believed entirely, and the first that frightened her more. Inside, the gallery smelled of oiled metal. Targets hung over painted mountains; rifles rested beneath red globes, their wooden stocks rubbed smooth. “Three shots,” the attendant announced. “Dime.” “Take the sailor doll,” Clara said. The stranger turned. “For me?” “For me. I want to see what your luck looks like when it isn’t impressing me.” “Charming. And here I thought we were being honest.” He raised a rifle. His easy posture vanished. The first shot rang; a tin bird dropped. “Two more,” said the attendant. “Time enough to change your mind about me?” “About the prize?” “About everything.” He missed the moon, then struck a star hidden behind it. A blue-eyed kewpie descended, swinging by one arm. “For the lady,” said the attendant. He handed it to Clara. “You may keep it. I dislike carrying things that can be lost.” “That sounds dangerously close to caring.” “Does it?” “About the doll.” A curl had fallen across his brow. She remembered *locks*: first hair, then fastenings. “Why me?” “Because you came.” “Anyone might, for a curiosity.” “No. They won’t.” He returned the rifle. She had begun, without noticing, to listen for cruelty in his words and find only kindness. That was less comforting. “He is like no one I remember,” she said. “No? You hardly remember anyone.” “That isn’t an answer.” “It is a fact.” “Why the shooting gallery?” “Because you like a spectacle, and because every man needs to prove himself before midnight.” “Did the letter promise you I’d come?” “No.” “Then why did you write?” His smile altered at its edges. “Because I needed you here.” “Need is an ambitious word.” “It is also a dangerous one.” He held the kewpie out of reach when she reached for it. “Ask me something else.” “Why do you keep giving me prizes I don’t want?” “Because you are not obliged to accept them.” A painted sailor hung crooked from the prize shelf, grinning into the electric light. She had come for an answer and was being handed a collection of beautiful irrelevancies. Yet his hand on hers felt unnervingly certain. “Walk with me,” he said. “To where?” “Only as far as the arch.” “No?” He glanced toward the thinning crowd. “You may watch the officers while I steal the kewpie.” “You won’t run?” “I have no reason to.” “I have no reason to trust that.” “A fair beginning.” He offered his arm. After a pause, she laid her gloved hand over it. Beneath the wool, his muscle was taut with an effort she suspected he did not intend to show. “Why are you afraid of me?” he asked. “I am not.” “No?” His gaze touched her mouth. “You keep glancing at the police as if they might rescue you from a particularly tedious stranger.” “I have been thinking of leaving.” “Most people are.” “What should I be thinking?” “That I am not a stranger.” “That is not an answer.” “It is the only one I can give safely.” Beneath the arch, the boardwalk narrowed. On the water, a steamer’s lights moved like a string of yellow beads. His fingers closed around hers, gentle as a decision, firm as a lock. “I saw you before,” he said. “Where?” “At this gallery. Long ago.” “I don’t believe you.” “That is not a complaint.” “Should it be?” “Most people who like me lie better.” “Who said I liked you?” “I did. Badly.” “You are remarkably sure of yourself.” “I learned from a better man.” “Who?” “The man I was before you.” “Perhaps I don’t trust him either.” His hand tightened almost imperceptibly. “No,” he said. “You shouldn’t.” She did not pull away.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates sophisticated craft in several areas while falling short in others. The author successfully captures the requested atmosphere of romantic allure with underlying danger, set against the evocative backdrop of 1937 Coney Island. The prose style is deliberately stylized, employing clipped dialogue and fragmented exposition that creates a noir-like quality appropriate to the period and mood. The dialogue is particularly strong, featuring sharp exchanges that reveal character while maintaining mystery. Lines like "You shouldn't say such things to a woman who can't remember her own" and "I learned from a better man... The man I was before you" demonstrate wit and psychological complexity. The conversation feels natural despite its heightened quality, with each character having a distinct voice. The mysterious elements are well-handled, particularly Clara's memory loss and the stranger's cryptic familiarity. The author plants intriguing details—the yellow hat, the music box, the repeated meetings—without over-explaining, maintaining tension throughout. The power dynamic between the characters feels authentically complex, with Clara maintaining agency despite her vulnerability. However, the piece suffers from some structural issues. The requested dialogue/monologue/exposition ratio appears unmet, with internal monologue being significantly less than the specified 20%. The memory fragments, while atmospheric, feel somewhat disconnected from the main narrative thread. Some descriptions veer toward the overwrought ("paper moons above the darkening sea"), though this generally serves the stylized tone. The characterization is nuanced, particularly in how Clara navigates her attraction to someone she simultaneously trusts and distrusts. The stranger remains appropriately enigmatic without becoming a cipher. Both characters feel like real people with complex motivations rather than genre archetypes. The ending maintains the established tension without false resolution, which is appropriate for what appears to be an early scene in a larger work. The final exchange about trust feels earned rather than forced. + Surreal horror: Caribou Season at the Lodge — Score: 83.0
Prompt:
Caribou Season at the Lodge Genre: Surreal Horror JT knew something wasn't right from the moment they'd pulled up to the lodge. It looked exactly as it had every autumn of his life—the cedar shingles silvered with age, the porch sagging gently under weight of winters past—but the air felt thicker, somehow, as if the woods had leaned in closer, waiting. He thought maybe he was just tired. Maybe it was nothing more than the long drive north, cramped in the back of the truck beside his older brother Mike -- and a stack of rifles wrapped in oily canvas. Still, the feeling lingered. The first caribou they found that season hadn't bolted. It had just watched, ears flicking lazily, waiting for the shot. JT had felt a crawling in his gut watching it die, noticing how it fell with a quiet dignity—as though it had wanted nothing more. Nobody else seemed to find it odd, or at least they didn't say so. JT kept his mouth shut. Always safer that way. Then there was the moment in the clearing. JT had fallen behind, fumbling with bootlaces stiff from the cold, and by the time he'd caught up with his father and brother, they'd already stopped. JT slowed instinctively, ducking behind a tangle of brush, staring out into the open space where a massive buck stood utterly still, chest rising and falling in slow, deep breaths. The animal looked…wrong, somehow. Maybe it was the eyes—dark and flat, calm in a way that made JT's neck prickle. Or maybe it was something deeper, something in the way the buck stood close enough for his father to reach out and touch it. JT watched as his father raised a trembling hand toward the animal's muzzle. His father's face had a strange expression, eyes too bright, lips parted slightly, like he was on the verge of whispering something—a secret, maybe. The rifle hung uselessly at his side, forgotten. Mike had the same dazed look in his eyes. JT's breath stopped short, his mind suddenly shouting at him to look away, turn around, just run—but he couldn't move. And then, as suddenly as it had begun, it was over. The buck shivered, startled by something unseen, and disappeared into the brush without so much as a sound. The two of them looked around, confused, seemingly surprised to find themselves where they stood. JT stayed hidden, breathing shallowly, fear mingling with a confused sense of shame. His father had failed to take the shot. To even think about mentioning what he'd seen would have felt like betrayal—or something worse. JT waited until the others moved on before stepping out from cover. He stared into the empty clearing for a long, uneasy moment, wondering if anything had really happened at all, or if he was losing his grip. Maybe the woods were finally getting into his head. Writing Instructions: Continue with the next chapter of the story, maintaining a style reminiscent of Stephen King—grounded realism blended seamlessly with unsettling surrealism. The atmosphere should convey subtle dread, isolation, and psychological ambiguity. JT's perspective is crucial, yet he is an unreliable narrator, caught in uncertainty about what he's perceiving. Establish an undertone of creeping dread, establishing the isolation of JT's perspective, which he largely keeps to himself. Incorporate some dialogue. Build tension towards a payoff. 1000 words.

## Chapter Two: Before the Moon By the time the coffee came to a boil, Roy Pyle had told us twice about the moon. He was a thin, red-cheeked man with bad boots and a red scarf wound twice around his neck. He had greeted us with the enthusiasm of someone selling kitchen cabinets, talking as he pointed out the woodpile, the game hooks beneath the porch, and the place where we were supposed to park. “The rain’s been late,” he said. “Deer are feeding high because of worms in the clover. Moon’ll be full Thursday night.” He said that last part while looking at me, though I hadn’t asked him anything. Dad glanced up from the stove. “The moon won’t interfere with our hunt.” “I didn’t say it would.” Roy laughed, showing a gap between his front teeth. “I said when you ought to be on the road home.” For all his talking, Roy wanted no company. He ate his breakfast on the tailgate of his truck, a hundred yards from the lodge. When Dad approached, Roy became fascinated by the sky, the tree line, or some difficult adjustment to his rifle. He spoke at us across the yard without seeming to expect an answer. I’d never known a man who could make small talk sound like a warning without actually warning you. That afternoon, I found him splitting kindling beside the woodpile. “You might as well talk,” he said before I could explain myself. “Standing over a man while he works makes him nervous.” “Sorry.” “Don’t be. Your father’s the one who should be sorry.” The axe stopped. “He put his hand on that animal,” Roy continued. “I saw him do it.” “I know.” “Did you?” “He touched its face.” Roy drove the axe into a round of wood with a dull crack. “Hands don’t interest me. I’m interested in what came along to put them there.” The woods clicked around us. A bird called somewhere high in the trees, and nothing answered. “What do you mean?” I asked. Roy split another piece, then another. “That buck asked your father something. Your father hasn’t answered out loud. That isn’t the same as saying no.” “He didn’t seem dangerous.” “Your father would say the same thing if the animal had a rifle.” I almost laughed. Roy didn’t. “He’s going to want to go back,” he said. “If either of you enters those trees after moonrise, don’t follow.” “Even Mike?” Roy looked at me then. “Most of all Mike.” “Mike hasn’t done anything.” “Not yet.” I thought he meant the moon. Roy straightened up. His hands were shaking, though the cold couldn’t explain it. He stuffed them into his jacket pockets. “If something calls you after dark, keep walking.” “What if it’s my father?” “Keep walking.” “What if it’s you?” Roy’s mouth tightened. For an instant, I thought he might tell me to keep walking into the woods and never come back. Instead, he said, “Especially then.” Then he went back to splitting wood, and I went inside to tell Dad we should leave early. He listened without looking up from his rifle. “After breakfast,” he said. “Let’s see how the hunting goes.” I never mentioned the guide’s warning. By dusk, Dad and Mike had seen six caribou. None of them bolted. They stood at the edge of the trails with their heads raised, watching us come, watching us stop. Dad lowered his rifle each time. Mike said one of the does looked tired. Dad agreed that they all did. None of them looked tired. They looked attentive. I told myself Dad was being patient. I told myself Mike was making jokes. I kept telling myself things while the rifles gathered dust, and the caribou watched, and the sky thickened overhead. Then Dad said we were going back to camp. On the path, Mike stopped beside me. “Did you see what it did?” “The buck ran when Dad raised his rifle.” “That’s not what I mean.” “What do you mean?” He looked toward the trees, but before he could answer, Dad called from ahead. Mike followed, and I was left standing there with my hands inside my sleeves, my heart beating like a trapped bird. None of us mentioned the clearing again. That was how I knew something had truly gone wrong. Not because of the caribou or Roy’s warnings, but because Dad and Mike had begun looking at me differently—as if they knew what I had seen and expected me to keep it to myself. Some part of me already did. I woke just after midnight. Nothing stood in the room. Nothing touched me. Nothing breathed against the window. That was the trouble: I expected something to be there. The moon had come out from behind the clouds, whitening the floorboards and the edges of the beds. Dad’s side of the room was empty. Mike’s bed had been thrown back. The front door stood open. I found my boots and went outside. Roy’s truck was gone. His chair sat beside the woodpile, dark with dew. Beyond the outbuildings, I could hear footsteps. They were not coming from the road. I don’t remember deciding to follow them. My feet chose the path through the birches, the same narrow trail Dad and I used to take to the swimming hole. My body knew where it went. My mind stayed several steps behind. The sounds led me to the clearing. Dad and Mike stood on the far side of it, so still that I mistook them for two weathered stumps. Between them waited the buck. It was larger than I remembered. Its antlers rose above the low branches, and its white breath moved slowly in the moonlight. Each time it exhaled, I smelled coffee. Roy stood nearby with his hat in his hands, staring down at the ground. Then the buck lifted its head. Its mouth did not move. “You can come out now,” it said. The voice came from everywhere: from the trees, from the antlers, from the hollow space behind my ribs. It sounded almost like mine. “You don’t have to hide what you saw.” I stayed behind the last birch. Dad had told me not to look at a wounded deer. I had obeyed him in the woods. I had obeyed him when I stayed hidden while he reached toward that buck’s muzzle. The silence afterward had felt like a promise I hadn’t meant to make. But this was different. This was the voice I had used in my own head all day, the quiet voice that said nothing had happened, that Dad was merely strange, that I had imagined everything because imagining was easier than being wrong. “It’s all right,” the buck said. “You can come with us.” Mike turned toward me. His face looked wet, though there were no tears on it. “Little brother,” he said. “You finally see it.” Dad’s gaze found me next. His expression was not empty. It was too full, too fixed, as though he was looking at me through glass. “Come here, JT,” he said. My feet moved before I could stop them. Roy’s voice cut across the clearing. “Don’t answer it.” The buck looked at me, and the woods went silent. I thought of all the things I might have said. I thought of Dad’s hand on its muzzle. I thought of my fear, and my shame, and the relief of having kept both to myself. Some part of me wanted to explain. I wanted to say that I hadn’t meant to leave them out there. I wanted them to tell me I hadn’t seen what I thought I had seen. The buck lowered its head. “We understand,” it said in my father’s voice. I nearly said *Thank you.* That was close enough. The word rose in my throat, and Dad took a step toward me. Mike caught his arm, but gently, the way you might stop someone from walking into a room where something fragile was waiting. The guide shouted my name. I ran. The path was straight. I kept my eyes on the pale strip of it and did not look at the trees. My lungs burned. The rifle stock knocked against my shoulder with every stride, and more than once I heard footsteps matching mine in the brush. When I reached the truck, I opened the driver’s door and climbed inside without looking at the back seat. The key was in the ignition, warm beneath my fingers. I don’t remember putting it there. The engine started on the first try. I shifted into reverse, backed out of the rut, and pointed the truck toward the south road. The headlights swept across the porch, the woodpile, Roy’s empty chair. I should have seen the guide. I should have seen Dad and Mike following. I saw neither. In the mirror, the trees slipped away beneath a pale moon. It hung above them, bright and fixed, as if the truck and the sky were moving at different speeds. “That’s all right, JT,” Dad said from somewhere behind me. “We understand.” I pressed my foot harder against the gas. I didn’t look back. It wasn’t courage. I was afraid that if I did, I would see them waiting for me—and worse, I would believe they forgave me.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong adherence to the Stephen King-inspired surreal horror brief, effectively maintaining JT's unreliable narrator perspective while building atmospheric dread. The author successfully captures King's signature blend of grounded realism with supernatural elements, particularly in the portrayal of ordinary hunting activities that gradually become sinister. The characterization is nuanced, with JT's internal conflict between loyalty to family and growing horror well-developed. Roy serves as an effective harbinger figure, delivering cryptic warnings that feel authentic rather than exposition-heavy. The dialogue feels natural and serves multiple purposes - advancing plot, revealing character, and building tension. Roy's laconic warnings ("Keep walking") are particularly effective. The prose quality is generally high, with strong atmospheric details like "the woods clicked around us" and "my heart beating like a trapped bird." The author avoids purple prose while maintaining evocative imagery. The pacing builds effectively toward the climactic clearing scene, where the supernatural elements fully emerge. The supernatural revelation is well-earned through careful buildup. The buck speaking in JT's voice, then his father's voice, creates genuine unease. The family's gradual enthrallment feels believable rather than sudden. JT's final escape maintains ambiguity about whether he's truly free, with his father's voice appearing in the truck. However, some elements feel slightly underdeveloped. Roy's disappearance is mentioned but not fully explored. The ending, while atmospheric, relies somewhat heavily on the "was it real?" ambiguity without quite earning the full emotional impact. Some transitions between scenes could be smoother. The piece succeeds in creating genuine dread and maintains consistent tone throughout. The horror emerges organically from family dynamics and isolation rather than relying on shock value. JT's perspective remains convincingly that of someone questioning his own perceptions while being drawn into something beyond his understanding. # Hell Is Other Demons At six-thirty, Lucifer Morningstar made coffee in a kitchen where no one was expecting him. The refrigerator hummed. Beyond the windows, the Lake of Fire burned in a modest strip of orange, because Hell had a noise ordinance. The penthouse had eleven bedrooms. Lucifer used two. The other nine were aired daily for guests, although he hadn’t had a guest in some time and preferred not to examine the discrepancy. Every Thursday, he set his phone to Do Not Disturb. This had nothing to do with Lilith. He checked that this remained true. It was Thursday. Three weeks ago, after another argument about a bridge, she had left through his office window. He had sent her the bill for the window. She had sent him the bill for the bridge. Neither bill had been paid. They were off again. He did not expect her. He simply kept Thursday free, a small administrative error that had recurred for several centuries. At nine, he went to work. Hell was administered from a basalt tower that had once been a mountain and was still disproportionately smug about it. Lucifer’s title was Chief Executive of Eternal Consequences. The position involved mostly forms. His crown sat on top of a filing cabinet. He considered this a matter of job security. His secretary, Mrs. Thrale, was a damned solicitor with immaculate handwriting. She had died during a disputed codicil and retained strong feelings about punctuation. She believed Lucifer’s crown and filing system posed a comparable threat to civilization. The morning brought forty-six appeals, a plumbing dispute involving the River Styx, and a request from Heaven to return all souls “currently on loan.” Heaven had not specified a return date. Hell could not establish that any souls had been borrowed. The request went into the pending pile, which was not known for its punctuality. At eleven, Gary, a former motivational speaker, appealed his sentence of listening to other people’s problems for eternity. “I’d like a transfer,” he said. “Somewhere quieter.” “There is a circle for the solitary,” said Lucifer. “That sounds ideal.” “We do a great deal of solitary.” Gary looked at the forms, then at the window, then at the lake. “How long does the transfer take?” “Forever.” “Send it in.” The appeal was denied. Gary said he understood. He did not understand. The sentence continued, which was the one advantage of eternity: there was always another seminar. At one, there were three knocks, a pause, and a fourth knock. Lucifer knew who it was before he opened the door. He was pleased, then immediately concerned that he was pleased, which was a familiar sequence and one he had never learned to enjoy. Lilith stood in the doorway wearing a charcoal coat and looking like a thundercloud that had been asked to fill out a form. In one hand she carried her scorched leather purse. It clinked as she entered: a plastic saint with one arm missing, a hotel key, a ticket stub whose title had worn away, a teaspoon from a seaside café. Lilith collected small things from the mortal world. When asked, she said they were portable. He had learned not to ask. “You look terrible,” she said. “I haven’t slept.” “That isn’t a diagnosis.” “No. It’s a schedule.” She put the purse on his desk and sat in his chair. He had replaced the chair since her last visit. It made no difference. “I came to return your pen,” she said, and held it out. “You stole that.” “I returned it. You’re confusing two events with a difference in tense.” “It’s my pen.” “It was in my possession.” “For six hundred years.” “I kept it safe.” He looked at the signature on his blotter, which was certainly his, except for a little extra flourish near the final letter. “You used it to sign a property transfer.” “I was making a point.” “With my name?” “Your pen. Your ink. Your inadequately guarded stationery.” The property was their old house in the Fourth Circle. The roof leaked, the garden was poisonous, and the gate he disliked was attached to a door she liked. Neither of them would sell. Their lawyers had made a career from the delay, though not the sort of career they had anticipated. “The deed,” he said. “I need your signature.” “You could have sent a lawyer.” “I could have.” “And?” “And I came here instead.” He found he had nothing to say. He had an empire, several languages, and a very good pen. None of these turned out to be useful. “What if I refuse?” he asked. “Then I keep the pen.” “That seems unjust.” “It’s the principle.” “It’s my pen.” “There you are.” She took it back and put it in her purse. The gesture was unreasonably satisfying. After a moment, he realized she had signed nothing at all. They argued about the gate instead. Then the garden. Then a chair that had survived three centuries of their disagreements and was, according to Lilith, hiding something. At four, he ordered dinner from a mortal bakery because Hell’s sandwich options had failed inspection. “There is cheese in the office,” he said. “Of course there is. This is Hell.” “There is also a sandwich.” “Who made it?” “The chef.” “Then it is not a sandwich. It is an administrative warning.” The food arrived forty minutes later. They ate noodles from paper cartons on his office floor, because the table was for negotiations and neither of them felt like negotiating. “You could come to the penthouse for coffee,” he said. “Why?” “The kettle is new.” “The last one whistled.” “It was the only thing you liked about it.” Her chipped mug was still at the back of the cupboard. He had never thrown it away. It seemed unnecessarily honest now that she had seen it. Lilith considered the invitation, or the kettle, or the eleven empty bedrooms. “All right,” she said. “But I’m not staying the night.” “I have an early meeting.” “Of course you do.” “Eleven o’clock.” “Your meetings used to start later.” “I’m working on my boundaries.” “I see that.” They took the lift up. On the way, she complained about the music. He explained that changing it would require cooperation. She said cooperation was not one of her professional strengths. At seven, she sat in the good chair. He sat in the other one. She did stay the night. It was only coffee, of course. She had a prior engagement, and he had a meeting, and the evening happened for reasons neither of them trusted. They watched a mortal film in which a family attempted to repair a lighthouse. Lilith said the engineering was implausible. Lucifer said the lighting was worse. They argued until one of them fell asleep, which was probably her. He woke at two to find her curled in the chair with one hand around his pen. Her purse rested beside her feet, emitting its faint smell of smoke and cloves. He put a blanket over her and returned to bed without waking her. In the morning, the pen would be on his desk. He made sure his diary was open to Friday.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece successfully captures the requested tone and style, drawing clear inspiration from Neil Gaiman's approach to blending the mundane with the fantastical. The image of Lilith sleeping with his stolen pen while he opens his diary to Friday suggests hope without guaranteeing resolution. Some minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the bureaucratic humor becomes slightly repetitive, and a few descriptions that could be more vivid. + Historical fiction: Gladiator — Score: 78.8
Prompt:
Historical Fiction: Write a scene from a story set during the height of the Roman Empire, focusing on a slice of a day in the life of a gladiator. Do not write a combat scene. Use sensory details to capture the sights, sounds, and smells of ancient Rome. Explore the gladiator's thoughts and emotions. The story should also touch on the larger political and social issues of the time period. The piece should feel like a slice of a larger story. First person, past tense, 1000 words.
Model Output:
## The Third Knot The day began with the scrape of a bucket against stone. Before dawn, Rome was more smell than sight. Through the dormitory wall came the splash of water, the ring of a barber’s shears, and someone swearing at a lamp that had gone out. Smoke seeped through our roof tiles, bitter with yesterday’s porridge. I lay on my pallet and listened to my ribs whistle, thinking that the silence after the bucket had never been silence at all. I was twenty-six, a murmillo, and a slave. I had not come to the Ludus Magnus for glory. I had come because the streets of Ostia were filling with men whose trades had failed or whose sons had been taken for Dacia, and because a hungry man could be bought for less than a pig. My father had died owing a baker. I was seventeen when the bailiff sold me. The Ludus at least promised regular porridge. I ate that porridge on a stone bench: thick barley, beans, and a heel of bread that scraped my throat. Across the yard, the blacksmith hammered helmet rims. He had no need for decoration. We were not soldiers. The state did not count our victories, and it would not inscribe our names on a monument. But if we pleased the aedile, he might purchase our freedom before the games ended. The wooden sword called the rudis was a poor reward for a life, but it was the only door I could see. Old Nicanor came for roll call, leaning on a stick that had once been a spear. He checked the straps of my helmet, the rim of my shield, and the place where my sword grip had begun to shine. Some of the men he had trained were dead now. He never softened that fact, and neither did he soften the arithmetic: a gladiator could win for years and leave no wife, no children, and no one left to mourn him. We were permitted to hope. That was how the Ludus kept us alive. By the third hour, the sun had reached the yard. I soaked in our bathhouse until the water softened my skin, then scraped away sweat and oil with a bronze tool. The heat brought out an old bruise over my ribs and the smell of every man in the room. On the walk back, the clean wool of my tunic already felt wrong against my skin. In my chest beneath it rested my sister’s last letter. Her words were blurred from much handling: my mother coughed through the winter; my brother’s unit had written that it was too dangerous to send news. No new letter would come today. At midday, we walked to the amphitheatre in formation. The bronze plates beneath my arms felt heavier in the heat. Along the route, the city smelled of hot bread, cabbage, incense, horse dung, and the sharp ammonia of fullers’ vats. Hucksters called their prices in Latin and Greek. Water sellers threaded between the crowds, and a flute player leaned from a balcony, playing as though the day belonged to someone else. On the Forum, officials posted notices about taxes, grain, and the levy for Dacia. People gathered around them, reading names, prices, and obligations in the same breath. Rome praised its soldiers and taxed its poor. It fed the hungry, too, but called the meal generosity. The games made both arrangements seem like peace. We passed men who had come to be seen as well as men who feared missing the free grain. A senator’s name might be announced before a single gladiator’s; his family sat apart from us, whitened by expensive dye. Yet our contracts belonged to the aedile, and if he lost office, they might be sold to another master. We depended on Rome’s favors while despising the hands that dispensed them. I hated the men in the shaded seats. I also hated how easily I watched for their approval. At the service gate, the noise of the street gave way to a hollow roar. The smell changed too: sweat, hot iron, animal waste, and the incense burning beside the statues of the gods. Beyond the gate, the sand shone pale and level. Dark patches marked where the day’s performers had already been used. We were not alone in being afraid, but fear was not permitted to slow us. Before every fight, I tied a red cord around my left wrist. Three knots: one for my mother, one for my brother, one for the life I meant to keep. My mother had tied the first knot before my first public performance. She had said it would bring me home. I knew cord could not turn an audience’s mercy, yet I continued to believe it. Each morning, I pulled it snug enough to feel my pulse, as if the beats belonged to her. Quintus, our lanista, checked our hands and sent us forward. The aedile sat in the white toga of his office, receiving the crowd’s applause as other men receive taxes. Some senators had come to watch; others had sent clients to count the applause. That was power: not the bronze helmet, but the ability to make thousands look the same way. The fear remained: that a mistake would be met not with anger but with hunger. I swallowed, waiting for the hush before my name. No god answered, and I was almost relieved. It meant the next breath, as always, belonged to me. Silence in front of thousands frightened me more than their shouts, because in that silence I was only a man with a borrowed name. My mouth was dry. I thought of my mother’s hands, and the white house I had once promised myself. Then the trumpet sounded, and the herald called my name. The crowd’s welcome struck me like wind against a shield. I touched the three knots one last time. The gate opened. Heat poured out, carrying blood, sand, and incense. I stepped into the light.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical competence and atmospheric writing within the historical fiction genre. The author successfully creates an immersive Roman setting through carefully chosen sensory details - the scrape of buckets, bitter smoke, the smell of fullers' vats, and the tactile sensation of bronze armor in heat. The first-person narrative voice is consistent and authentic, capturing the resigned pragmatism of a gladiator who views his profession as economic necessity rather than heroic calling. The characterization is nuanced and believable. The protagonist emerges as neither a stereotypical noble warrior nor a bitter victim, but rather a practical man caught in circumstances beyond his control. His conflicted feelings toward the Roman elite - simultaneously despising and seeking their approval - ring psychologically true. The detail of the three-knotted cord provides effective emotional grounding without sentimentality. The piece successfully integrates period-appropriate political and social commentary, touching on taxation, military conscription for Dacian campaigns, grain distribution, and class divisions. These elements feel organic to the narrative rather than forced exposition. The writing demonstrates sophisticated understanding of Roman society's complexities. However, the piece suffers from some structural weaknesses. The pacing feels somewhat uneven, with the middle section becoming slightly meandering as it moves through the day's routine. While the sensory details are generally effective, some passages veer toward overwrought description that slows momentum. The ending, while atmospheric, lacks a strong sense of completion or revelation that would elevate it beyond competent scene-setting. The prose occasionally becomes too dense with metaphorical language, particularly in passages like "Rome was more smell than sight" and "listened to my ribs whistle." While these moments show literary ambition, they sometimes feel forced rather than natural. The piece also relies heavily on telling rather than showing in certain sections, particularly when explaining the gladiator's backstory and the political situation. Despite these issues, the writing demonstrates genuine skill in voice, atmosphere, and character development. The emotional complexity feels earned rather than manufactured, and the historical setting is convincingly rendered without falling into cliché.
